articles.content: New tariffs planned as Trump administration clamps down on ‘unfair trade practices’ Hannah Webster , senior economist at the think tank New Economics Foundation , also called for other measures. The price cap increase will be difficult news for households to bear, especially during the winter when our energy needs and bills are higher. The government’s current support measures don’t match the reality of rising costs and squeezed household finances. The £100 payment announced at the budget won’t cover the increase that’s coming, nor is it available to every household. According to NEF analysis, one million low-income households will miss out. Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home. Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Early in the second half of Tuesday night’s National League South match between Torquay United and Chesham, play was briefly suspended due to an ear-splitting din emitted over the Plainmoor public address system. “The game has stopped because the Torquay Tannoy system is making a loud noise that won’t stop,” posted Chesham on their Social Media Disgrace account. “I’m not kidding.” A sort of aural cross between an ocean liner’s foghorn and a party conference speech delivered by a senior member of the Reform party, it eventually stopped and play resumed with Torquay running out 2-1 winners. In this constantly changing world of global disruptions, uncertainties and risks, with social, political and economic disaffection seemingly on the rise everywhere, it’s genuinely heartening to know that some things never change . ‘Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose’, as the late, great French writer Jean-Baptiste Alphonse Karr famously said, something that I’m sure Big Dunc is well aware of” – Noble Francis. May I be the 1,092nd correspondent to demand a review of the Letter o’ the Day award for Monday – and it be awarded to Declan Hackett for his letter foretelling the rescinding of the red card given to Lenny Yoro on Sunday? Given the precedent of awarding/revoking/re-awarding of the Afcon 2025 edition this would be entirely justified” – Peter Martin. This is an extract from our daily football email … Football Daily. To get the full version, just visit this page and follow the instructions . Continue reading...

articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.content: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Beasley
articles.content: While referees tend to reach for red early in the season before easing off, players are under increasing pressure to keep pace in a frenetic environment Off! Off! Off! The past three Premier League games have featured a red card, each for a different reason. Brighton’s Costinha was sent off for two bookings at Hull , Leny Yoro collected a red card against Liverpool for denying a goalscoring opportunity ( though his suspension was overturned on appeal ) and James Tarkowski saw red for serious foul play at Brentford . This season is shaping up to be an outlier in the VAR era of officiating in English football. The latest red cards took the Premier League total to 22 in 2026-27. The rate of 0.2 per game equates to 76 across the whole season, which would equal the Premier League record set in 2005-06. Refereeing has evolved in the past decade, though. The average across the seven completed campaigns since VAR was introduced is 0.12 per game, with a high of 0.15 in 2023-24. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alaina Demopoulos
articles.content: A generation known for loneliness is putting their own spin on a millennial-made tradition that requires socializing It’s a TikTok scene straight out of a stress dream: two men stand in their freshly cleaned apartment, explaining how all but one of the people they invited to Friendsgiving flaked out at the last minute. There is a can of whipped cream on the table and a 6lb ham in the oven. According to the video, posted by pop-culture podcaster Jackson Strike, those who ditched were either tired, or sick, or had a difficult day at work. More than 1.5 million people liked the video and many flooded to the comments section to express their disappointment at what they saw as an epidemic of antisocial behavior. “Everyone wants a village until they have to be a villager,” one user wrote. “Time to get new friends,” quipped another. Continue reading...

articles.author: Martin Pegan
articles.content: One or perhaps more spots are up for grabs ahead of the summer series against New Zealand. We assess the leading batters’ chances of being picked in the XI Australia’s cricketers would be within their rights to be counting down the days until attention turns to the first Test of the home summer against New Zealand in Perth. As the sandpapergate scandal overshadows a pair of white-ball series against arch-rivals England, batters around the country have been pressing their claims for a place in Australia’s XI when the Chappell-Hadlee Trophy series begins on 9 December. A vacancy has already opened at the top of the order after selectors took the unusual step to confirm earlier this month that Marnus Labuschagne had been dropped from the squad for the four-Test series. The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests. Continue reading...

The race to replace Australia’s No 3 – whether slotting straight into Labuschagne’s spot at first drop or as part of a batting order reshuffle – has become packed with Test discards and an emerging talent hoping to earn a debut. The door could open for more than one addition to the XI alongside presumed incumbents Travis Head, Matt Renshaw, Steve Smith, Cameron Green, Josh Inglis and wicketkeeper Alex Carey, with worrying signs Australia’s ageing squad is starting to creak after three defeats in their past five Tests. articles.content: The job of Mauricio Pochettino’s successor is to fine-tune a team on the up. That requires a bureaucrat rather than a figurehead First, let’s get the Pep Exception out of the way. Or perhaps we’d better call it the Guardiola Caveat. Regardless, the point is the same. If US Soccer can get Pep Guardiola to manage the United States men’s national team, it should. Because when you have the chance to employ the most successful and influential coach of his generation, the thinker who stands upstream of essentially every major tactical current of the last two decades, you just have to do it. But let us assume that US Soccer can’t appoint Guardiola, because he is only a few months into his post-Manchester City sabbatical and still busying himself defending his body of work . Because he has given no recent indication that he wants the job, even though he spent a previous break between managerial gigs living in New York City and was probably only being supportive of his newly-appointed colleague Mauricio Pochettino when he called the project “fascinating” two years ago. Also because he has only ever signed on to coach teams stacked with Ballon d’Or contenders, posing a Phil Jackson-type, bar-room question over whether he would still be exceptional in charge of unexceptional players. Continue reading...

articles.content: Vivienne Foroughirad/Texas A&M/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project In the turquoise waters of Western Australia’s Shark Bay lives a large resident population of dolphins. Some of these marine mammals are 54 years old, others just infants. But no matter their age, they live highly social lives. Researchers have studied these dolphins for decades . Forty years on, our extensive dataset reveals crucial insights into how these animals socialise throughout their lives – and how their social choices affect their health and fitness. In our new study , published in PLOS Biology, we analysed nearly 40 years of data on over 450 wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops aduncus ) from Shark Bay. We found that as dolphins navigate their social world, they develop unique personalities and social preferences, and individuals who are consistent about these preferences may live longer. Sociality is a spectrum Dolphins’ social lives mirror our own in remarkable ways. As they navigate their blue world, dolphins move in and out of social groups, constantly making decisions about who to spend time with and who to avoid, depending on the task at hand. Much like humans, dolphins vary markedly in how social they are. Research shows some are more cliquish, while others are true social butterflies, embedded in large and complex social networks These differences matter. Just as in humans and many other species, the way dolphins navigate their social lives can shape their survival, longevity and reproductive success. For example, strong social connections promote resilience, while social isolation can increase mortality risk . Such patterns are not set in stone either. In many species , including humans, social behaviour is shaped as we age. In humans, social networks often become smaller, with older adults becoming more selective, investing their time and energy in a smaller number of meaningful relationships. But what happens as dolphins age? Previous research on dolphins has shown us that extended maternal care in older dolphin mothers is evidence of reproductive senescence – similar to menopause in humans. This raises an intriguing question: do dolphins also show other patterns of ageing like our own? Drone footage of six individuals who reside in nearshore habitat off the coast of Monkey Mia, Shark Bay. In front from left to right are Risotto (24) and her calf, Linguini (2), who is in a nursing position; Whoops (27), and Wags (6). Behind them are two more individuals; Risotto’s previous calf Arancini (6), and Jungle (8). Diana Alvarado/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project , CC BY Social ageing can be measured in multiple ways As we age, we develop personalities, build and lose relationships, and create our unique social environment which changes with each passing year. This process of social change as we grow is called social ageing . Most studies of social ageing have examined how individuals change over time by collecting many measurements, then finding their average. This can be useful for dolphins that have only a few close companions. But for those who frequently join groups large and small, an average tells us very little. We can instead turn to another measurement: predictability . This describes the spread of an individual’s data. Those dolphins who consistently spend time with the same number of other dolphins are very predictable. Those who flit between groups of many sizes are much less predictable. Predictability is difficult to measure because it requires a single individual be measured dozens, even hundreds, of times. Luckily, with 40 years of data on over 450 dolphins, research can go beneath the surface to study not only how individuals change in sociability with age on average, but how predictable they are, and if predictability can change, too. Being consistent is key For our new study, we examined the effects of sex, age, and individual personality on group size (a measure of sociability) throughout the population of dolphins at Shark Bay. We discovered several key points. First, dolphins follow a pattern very similar to humans and other long-lived species: they increase their average group size with age, to a point. After that point, which is unique to each individual, those average group sizes begin to decrease. Second, regardless of what their average group size is, individuals become more predictable with age. Third, males had a higher average group size and higher predictability than females. Finally, individuals who continued to increase their group size average and predictability most with age lived longer. Social stability can being a sustaining force Our research into dolphins’ social lives suggests that developing a strong and stable social environment can buffer many of the effects of ageing and enhance lifespan. Studying dolphins’ social traits reveals that it’s not only average behaviour which shapes fitness outcomes, but individual predictability. To truly understand how ageing shapes us, we must look beyond the average to see how the predictability of our social decisions can affect us as we navigate our world. This study reinforces the importance of maintaining consistent social relationships throughout the ageing process. In the case of the Shark Bay dolphins, it’s not only about how large one’s social circle is; rather, it’s about the social circle staying roughly the same size and type over size. And this holds an important lesson for us, because the trends we find in dolphins closely parallel the sort of patterns we see in human social behaviour as well. This project has received grant funding from the National Science Foundation and the US Office of Naval Research, as well as material support from the Royal Automobile Club Monkey Mia Resort. Celine Frere receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the US National Science Foundation. Janet Mann receives funding from The National Science Foundation for the long-term Shark Bay dolphin research.

articles.author: Anna Spargo-Ryan
articles.content: Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s tribute to Molly Meldrum contained heaps of the right words. But they were written by something that can’t feel I know how this will sound but when my nanna died the second thought I had, after utter devastation, was: “This is a writer’s dream.” She was 101. That is so many years old. I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her. The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum , by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done. Continue reading...

The Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson’s team took a similar approach in this week’s tribute to the music legend Molly Meldrum , by which I mean they generated it with AI. I imagine the conversation went something like: we are 25 years old, who even was she? And then one of them plugged Molly’s name into Claude while the others went downstairs for $11 coffees. Job done. Continue reading...

articles.content: Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg – who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024 – would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut. To “buy a seat” on a space mission, Australia has to make a financial contribution to the ESA. The precise sum is not public, but reports claim it could exceed the A$100 million mark . There has been interest in the press and excitement among space advocates. Many are pointing out that sending a home-grown astronaut to space would yield potential benefits to industry and the nation as a whole, inspiring younger generations. There would be a powerful symbolism in sending an Australian woman to space. However, while human spaceflight can deliver substantial benefits, it’s costly. As we’re in the midst of a substantial public campaign to #FlyKatherine , it’s crucial to properly analyse some of the claims being made about the potential benefits of such an expensive proposal. What counts as an Australian astronaut? The discussion raises an interesting point about what constitutes an Australian astronaut. To date, five Australian-born people have flown to space, two as NASA astronauts and three privately. The most recent was physicist Elaine Hyde, the first Australian woman in space . But her 2025 Blue Origin flight was privately funded, and she hasn’t been given the label of the first “female Australian astronaut”. The federal government hasn’t signalled a strong interest in flying an Australian astronaut. Science minister Tim Ayres unequivocally said state and territory governments and private industry would have to pitch in. However, only South Australia has agreed to contribute; industry has pledged up to $6 million. The Northern Territory called the proposal “ reckless ”. These debates are not new. In the 1980s, the Hawke government announced it would send an Australian astronaut on the space shuttle. However, then Minister for Science, Barry Jones, noted it wasn’t a high priority . Prestige and public relations were not considered reason enough when government spending was to be reined in. The cost would be substantial We don’t know if Australians would support spending $100m on a single space mission while facing a cost-of-living crisis. When surveyed in 2025, 51.5% of Australians supported government investment in an astronaut programme, but respondents were not given a cost. Generally speaking, once government programs reveal their costs , public support decreases. When asked in 2023 , more Australians supported the cancellation of a $1.2 billion Earth observation satellite than disagreed with it being canned. Would these funds be better deployed within the space sector? Currently the Australian Space Agency’s funding is $21.7m over two years. The cost of flying a single Australian astronaut would fund a decade for the agency. Put another way, $100m is half of the total government investment in space or space adjacent companies in the last 18 months. Space science and research occurs at universities, in government agencies, and in private industry; many organisations have sent experiments to space, often relatively cheaply. Advocates have argued there would be significant benefits to Australia. There’s no doubt space is of immense benefit to industry and the nation, from banking to navigation to farming . An astronaut can’t meet all these needs, and we don’t know how they fit into our long-term plans. Australia doesn’t have a whole of government space policy and an astronaut is not a space program. The suggestion that Australia’s growing space industry would stand to gain similarly deserves deeper analysis. How and where specifically will funds flow back to Australia? Does the public think supporting industry is a reason to send an astronaut to space? ESA has a geographic return policy which sees member states receive industrial contracts proportional to how much they pay ESA. But Australia is not a paying member state, and not looking to be. The $100 million includes training, equipment and launch; it’s difficult to see how the bulk of those funds will be spent in Australia rather than in Europe, where ESA is based. What about inspiration? Representation matters, particularly for encouraging girls and young women to pursue careers in space. Bennell-Pegg’s selection and training have already inspired Australians across the country. However, research shows that when role models in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) fields have seemingly unattainable careers, they actually make students less motivated to pursue STEM. The selection process was not nationally competitive and there’s no currently published plan or pathway for a young girl in Australia to follow in Bennell-Pegg’s footsteps. What message does that send to young people? It might discourage them from pursuing careers in space. We shouldn’t ignore the fact many Australians would support sending an astronaut simply because it’s exciting. That is a legitimate foundation for policy – after all we fund the arts, entertainment industry and sport – but we should also recognise many Australians would not agree with such spending when it comes to space. Unanswered questions remain If we want to send an astronaut to space, the Australian public should know precisely what the tangible benefits are – to them, their economy and their sense of what Australia stands for. A key final question is: what next? There are currently no plans for Australia to send a second astronaut to space after Bennell-Pegg. Not only does this limit the pathway for future Australians to go to space, but also undermines the arguments put forward for an Australian astronaut. If the benefits are so tangible and important, we wouldn’t only do it once. Kathryn Robison receives funding from the Department of Defence and is the Deputy President of Women In International Security Australia Inc. (WIIS-A). Tristan Moss receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the Department of Defence.

articles.author: Nick Ames at the Etihad Stadium
articles.content: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. Continue reading...

articles.author: Ed Aarons at Emirates Stadium
articles.content: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. Continue reading...

articles.author: Jen Sherman
articles.content: The US has more big chains but in Australia produce is better quality – and bread doesn’t taste like cake I poked. I pulled. I looked in confusion at the head of garlic I was holding, wondering why the cloves weren’t coming apart. When I dug my nails in and finally broke out a clove, its skin was pierced and there were scratch marks in the flesh. It had only been a few weeks since I moved back to Australia from the US, after a 10-year stint in San Diego; only a few weeks since I cooked with garlic cloves. Surely I hadn’t lost finger strength that quickly? Turns out, it wasn’t me. It was the garlic. Since that first Australian head of garlic, I’ve discovered that Australian garlic is tighter than the US variety. Over there, a few gentle rubs prise the cloves apart. Here, you’ve really got to put some effort in – I suspect that’s why you can buy a packet of garlic cloves in supermarkets and I never saw such a product in the States. Garlic in Australia is more expensive, too. Continue reading...

Now it plans to switch its primary stock market listing to New York in 2028. Compass is a bad one for the London market to lose. Second, its reasons for joining the stateside listing rush feel flimsy – but also dangerous. Continue reading...

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.content: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100th anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. Continue reading...

articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Sometimes, the beautiful game can make Football Daily feel old. Even Monday’s ostensibly old-school fixture between Brentford and Everton felt like the future destroying the past. The analytics-coded hosts prevailed 4-0 and James Tarkowski was dismissed by the VAR overlords for a challenge that would have been considered “firm but fair” on the muddy pitches of our youth. “I don’t think you can tackle like that in this day and age,” a misty-eyed David Moyes sighed after the game, before heading to the team bus to rewatch the Battle of Santiago . If Sunday was Gary Neville’s Sistine Chapel [ Monday’s Football Daily ], then his commentary on the Fernando Torres goal for Chelsea against Barcelona must be his David ” – Ronnie McMahon. Regarding Declan Hackett’s assertion [ Monday’s letters ] that Donald Trump will be helping his mate Mauricio Pochettino by ringing the FA to overturn Lenny Yoro’s red card, perhaps Poch should be careful what he wishes for: Trump may equally decide to get Michael Carrick reinstated, as he also has a bit of previous for that sort of thing” – Dexter O Riordan. In all the time that I have been watching football, I don’t think I have ever seen a player dismiss himself and be away down the tunnel before given a red card. Thanks James Tarkowski ” – Nigel Sanders. Brighton had only failed to win twice in the league since 5 September. A 1-1 draw with Leeds and a 2-0 defeat at Liverpool - their only opponents with double letters in their name. That bizarre hoodoo struck again at Hull on Sunday. Good good news for Seagulls fans is the only double-lettered encounters they have before hosting Hull in February are trips to Forest and Spurs. Even better news is that since that 1-1 draw with Leeds on 5 September, they have a 100% win record against sides without double letters and have not conceded a goal” – Dan Ashley (and no others). Continue reading...

articles.content: When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit . It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did. Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4. Continue reading...

articles.content: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.content: As he continues a foray into broadcasting with Netflix’s Thanksgiving Eve game, the Philadelphia folk hero reflects on fatherhood, flow states and outdueling Tom Brady Ask Nick Foles what he remembers most vividly about winning Super Bowl LII and he doesn’t mention the Philly Special , the brazen gadget play that passed straight into football folklore. Not the record 1,151 yards of combined offense or the nerve-shredding go-ahead touchdown drive or the surreal theater of a second-string quarterback outdueling Tom Brady on the biggest stage in American sports. Not even the moment Brady’s last-gasp Hail Mary pass fell harmlessly to the turf and the Philadelphia Eagles became champions of the National Football League for the first time since the Eisenhower administration. Instead, he remembers holding his daughter. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alyssa Mercante
articles.content: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA VI’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%. Continue reading...

articles.author: Aaron Timms
articles.content: For big stars, endorsing companies like Kalshi and Polymarket is just another day in the beautiful business of being – and staying – rich When Giannis Antetokounmpo announced he was taking an investment stake in prediction market Kalshi in February, the claim he made to accompany the announcement – “We all on Kalshi now” – sounded as absurd as the howls of outrage from sports lovers seemed universal. Nine months later, Kalshi’s grip on American fans appears murderously tight: notional monthly trading volume on the platform, the majority of which is taken up by wagers on sports, increased to nearly $100bn in October from $40bn in August, as the company gears up for yet another funding round at a rumored valuation of $65bn ahead of a potential IPO. Rival prediction market Polymarket, which relaunched in the US late last year after regulators shut it down in 2022, has seen similar growth over recent months. However righteous the disgust from fans on social media at the deepening incursion of these odious platforms into professional sport may be, their popularity seems only to grow. More perplexing is the widening circle of athletes like Giannis who’ve thrown off whatever shame might once have come from association with these businesses and given them their full-throated support. The line between role model and shill in professional sports is now essentially non-existent. Pete Sampras, a man so private in retirement it can often seem like his entire tennis career was a collective hallucination, released an ad for Kalshi during this year’s US Open after two decades largely out of the public eye. José Mourinho trousered a brick of Kalshi cash this summer in exchange for a gambling promo during the World Cup. The prediction market machine now sponsors Jalen Brunson and Josh Hart’s Roommates Show, on which the recently crowned pair of NBA champions begin every episode dutifully informing us that their amazingly dreary podcast is “presented by Polymarket, the top prediction market”. LeBron James will make more from his recently announced partnership with Polymarket – $15m a year – than he will from playing for the Philadelphia 76ers. Somehow we’ve arrived at the point where it’s bigger news if a professional athlete takes a firm stand against the prediction markets, as Victor Wembanyama recently did , rather than pockets the cash to endorse them. Continue reading...

articles.author: Luke Entwistle
articles.content: Winger has not played for the USMNT since the World Cup and believes good club form is his route back into the squad This was the USMNT’s summer. By extension, it was also that of the 26 players selected by Mauricio Pochettino to represent the nation at a home World Cup. It didn’t live up to expectations for all of them, and certainly not for Timothy Weah. “Obviously this summer wasn’t the best for me,” he says. Weah was one of eight players in the squad to have started all four of the US’s matches in Qatar in 2022. He remained a regular heading into this tournament but would ultimately start only one game in a campaign that came to an end at the hands of Belgium in the last 16 . “In every career you have moments where you’re a bit down, and you’re a bit in your head about things. I think the World Cup was definitely that for me,” Weah says. “On a personal level, I had to take a back seat and figure out where my place was in the squad.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers , but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. I think it’s a bit of a symbol of the quite extraordinary volatility, unpredictability that we’re seeing play out in markets in the AI sector, but more broadly as well. Continue reading...

articles.author: Beejay Silcox
articles.content: The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation. We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.” Continue reading...

articles.content: The Australian government has secured an agreement with the Greens to guarantee passage of its long-awaited digital duty of care bill . The bill puts the onus on big-tech companies to address foreseeable online harms. Announced on Tuesday, the deal includes a number of measures to strengthen the bill, including bigger fines for platforms (to as much as 5% of global revenue) and a private right for people to sue the companies that breach their duty of care. Federal Minister for Communications Anika Wells acknowledged that it’s impossible to “cure” the internet of its ills. But she emphasised the digital duty of care bill provides basic safety standards that have to date been lacking. She described the package as “ seismic reform ”. What exactly is a ‘digital duty of care’? At its core, the bill requires the person responsible for an online service to ensure – as much as is reasonably practicable – a safe online environment . That phrase is borrowed from workplace health and safety law, and the logic is similar: rather than waiting for harmful content to be reported and taken down, platforms must identify the risks their services create and act to reduce them. The duty replaces the existing industry codes – which Wells described as “ drafted by big tech for big tech ” – as well as the eSafety Commissioner’s Basic Online Safety Expectations . Under the new bill, platforms would have to complete annual written risk assessments, keep them for six years and produce them to the eSafety Commissioner on request. The legislation has been years in the making. A statutory review of the Online Safety Act, delivered in October 2024, made 67 recommendations to strengthen the law. Its central one was a single, overarching “duty of care”, which the government committed to. After nearly two years, the government released an exposure draft in September, the headline feature of which was an “ off switch ” for personalised, algorithm-driven feeds for users. The bill was introduced to parliament on October 15. A Senate committee then reviewed the bill, receiving 182 submissions. Last week, it released its recommendations, which included a civil right of action and an exemption for low-risk services, such as small business websites. It backed passage of the bill, subject to its recommendations. What are the new changes? Wells outlined seven new changes to the bill as part of the government’s deal with the Greens: a private right of action, allowing individuals and groups to sue platforms that breach the duty stronger privacy protections expanded powers for eSafety to remove nudify services the naming of addictive platform design features as a specific risk that platforms must assess a clarified definition of “hostile attitudes to women”, which Wells said targets content promoting hatred, violence and threats, not disagreement with feminism a rule-making power to create an external dispute resolution pathway higher fines for violations of the law. The penalty change is the headline amendment. The bill already carried a maximum penalty of about A$109 million for companies found to have breached the obligation. The amendment adds an alternative penalty of up to 5% of global revenue. Among jurisdictions with similar laws, this would place Australia between Canada at 3% and the European Union at 6%. The Greens had sought 10% . The dispute resolution pathway is what the Greens call a pathway to an independent ombudsman for big tech. It creates a three-tiered option for social media users to bring complaints of harms against tech companies. First, they can turn to the platforms’ internal complaint process. If that fails, they can complain to a yet-to-be established tech platform ombudsman. Then if that fails, they can use the private right of action to go to court. The duty of care law would go into force after a 12-month transition. The government has confirmed low-risk, small businesses will be exempted from the law through rules, rather than in the bill itself. A significant shift There are several reasons why the changes to the bill are significant. First, the private right of action changes who enforces the law. Until now, online safety regulation in Australia has depended almost entirely on the eSafety Commissioner’s resources and priorities. A statutory duty that individuals and groups of people can use to sue means platforms face litigation risk, as well as regulatory risk. That matters because suing platforms has been difficult. For example, Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest’s case against Meta over scam advertisements had to be pursued in a US court. Wells argued that Australians have previously had to attach claims to existing laws in order to sue. The new law would create a cause of action that does not currently exist. However, she said she expects it to be used rarely. Much will depend on how the courts approach causation in these types of cases, and on whether those financially backing litigation see class actions against platforms as viable. Second, the revenue-based fine raises the stakes with Washington. Wells said she met the US ambassador on Tuesday morning and acknowledged “points of difference” on this clause. She noted that courts elsewhere have rarely imposed maximum penalties against companies. The 5% figure is a ceiling, not a starting point. Third, the politics have changed. The Coalition opposes the bill, and Wells noted it will be the first online safety law to pass without bipartisan support. Online safety has been a rare area of consensus in Australia in the past. If the Coalition votes against the law, it is more exposed to being unwound, or simply under-resourced, after a change of government. Much of the detail is still to come. The dispute resolution scheme, the small business exemption and the treatment of addictive design all depend on rules yet to be written and on eSafety’s judgement. Regardless, with the passage of the bill now secured, the duty of care will shift responsibility to the companies that build these services. Rob Nicholls is a member of the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance. He receives funding from the ARC. He made a submission to, and appeared before, the Senate committe.

articles.author: Adrian Horton
articles.content: The Summer I Turned Pretty’s Christopher Briney and 1923’s Michelle Randolph try their best, but this chaotic cross-country journey is not worth taking Credit where credit is due: it takes some nerve for Amazon to open its latest holiday romcom, Clashing Through the Snow, with characters bemoaning the enervated state of the book industry. Publishing isn’t the cultural epicenter it once was, reports boutique press head Jeremy (PJ Byrne) before announcing some impending new year’s layoffs. Alas, things have changed – “if Faulkner were alive today, he’d be making ASMR videos with Mr Beast” (or, perhaps, competing on Prime Video’s Beast Games?) Self-awareness can be key to the ludicrous joys of a Christmas romcom confection, though Clashing Through the Snow, starring 1923’s Michelle Randolph and homegrown Amazon star Christopher Briney (The Summer I Turned Pretty), tests one’s patience for beating you to the branded punchline. Briney’s Ryan, a numbers-driven, macro-counting kind of book editor, pitches a “financial trends with benefits” romance that could be “Rebecca Yarros big”. Soulmates, says Randolph’s rival workhorse editor Hannah, are as mythical as “ethical billionaires and pain-free bikini waxes”. Due to said budget cuts, both have a week to land “a book so big it makes Harry Potter look like a Buzzfeed listicle” for only one to keep their job. What are two LA workaholics going to do on Christmas but take meetings in New York? Continue reading...

articles.content: As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. articles.content: The evidence seems overwhelming, but artists and writers have borrowed from each other for hundreds of years. The line between homage and theft is a thin one “Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal,” the poet TS Eliot wrote a century ago. No work of art, he argued, exists in a vacuum. Great writers draw on what came before them, transforming their influences into something entirely their own. Eliot’s words came to mind when I read the revelations about the queen of the country house bonkbuster Jilly Cooper, who has been accused of “extensive and deliberate” plagiarism in her 1978 book Prudence. At least 35 passages appear to have been lifted from The Serial, a satirical novel by American writer Cyra McFadden, alongside remarkable similarities to sections of Josephine Tey’s 1948 novel The Franchise Affair. McFadden’s daughter is threatening legal action, describing the treatment of her mother’s work as “unconscionable”. Nadia Khomami is arts and culture correspondent at the Guardian Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.author: Jonathan Wilson
articles.content: The manager’s first game in charge was a disaster and he needs to lift the mood within a sunken squad if a relegation battle is to be avoided Sign up for our free newsletter here In as much as any derby can ever be a free hit, there was always a sense that Mauricio Pochettino’s first game as Manchester United manager wouldn’t matter too much; nobody expected them to win away to Liverpool. This was not a game on which anybody was going to judge him, and that feeling only magnified when Leny Yoro was sent off after eight minutes. United’s victory at Anfield last season was their first for a decade; what’s difficult to do with 11 men is only going to get harder playing a man down for 82 minutes. But that does not mean that it did not matter. Although Roy Keane was determined to reject the suggestion, there was perhaps even some credit to be gleaned from having lost only 4-0 . Certainly when they were 2-0 down after 13 minutes, there was reason for United to fear an embarrassment akin to their 7-0 defeat against Liverpool in 2023 . Perhaps Pochettino deserves credit for his switch to a back three, which brought a degree of stabilisation, but United could easily have lost far more comfortably than they did. Liverpool had 18 shots in the game three-and-a-half years ago, eight of them on target; on Sunday they had 28, 11 of them on target. When you’ve conceded an xG of 4.38, there’s not much point quibbling over the details; you’ve been hammered. Continue reading...

articles.content: Royal & Derngate, Northampton The Black Books star gets off to a promising start as he contemplates ‘the burning ball of what you don’t understand’ but his search for levity leads to half-baked ditties Is Dylan Moran joking when he opens his show by telling Northampton’s audience “I didn’t write anything, or prepare”? By the end, you wouldn’t bet on it. Bleary directionlessness may be par for the course for the Irish comic, whose work has always combined poetic-philosophical dazzle with a certain wooziness. But after a promising start tonight, his new touring show, Looking for Trouble, conspicuously loses its way, as Moran frets about forgetting a significant chunk of material, before abandoning his encore and leaving a bewildered audience in his wake. That’s a shame, because there are shards of trademark brilliance in the opening 20 minutes, which see the 55-year-old address himself, albeit obliquely, to the mysteries of being human in 2026, AKA “the burning ball of what you don’t understand” From Trump to AI, Moran surveys it all in wide angle not closeup, as symptoms of our confusion, atavism and fear of expulsion from the tribe. The quality of his thinking in this section, while cheerfully offering himself up as Exhibit A in this prosecution of humanity’s perplexity, is arresting. And there are zingers, too, including a word-picture of the genitals that, once heard, may never be forgotten. Continue reading...

articles.author: Alexis Petridis
articles.content: The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along. The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation. Continue reading...

articles.content: Irina/Getty Images Have you ever wondered why restaurants include outrageously expensive bottles of wine on their menus? Often, those bottles aren’t expected to sell. Instead, they make the other wines seem better value even if they are still overpriced. By changing the context of the decision, the out-of-reach expensive option can nudge customers towards wanting the cheaper option more. Marketers use similar tricks all the time. A holiday package that’s sold out, a premium subscription nobody really wants, or a product that’s clearly overpriced can all influence how we perceive the alternatives around them. Behavioural economists call these influences “decoy effects” . They reveal that decisions are not always rational based on absolute value. Instead, they are often shaped by the options available at the time. Humans aren’t the only animals making decisions. Every day, wild animals weigh up risks and rewards: whether to investigate a novel object, where to forage, or whether entering a trap is worth the potential danger. That got us wondering: could a decoy influence a rat? That was the subject of our new study, published today in The Journal of Applied Ecology . The problem with trapping rats Rats are among the world’s most successful and adaptable animals. They damage crops and infrastructure, spread disease, threaten native wildlife and cost economies billions of dollars every year in damages and pest control. Despite more than a century of innovation and thousands of patented trap designs, trapping still depends on one crucial step: the animal must choose to enter the trap. This seemingly simple decision is often where pest control programs fail. Many rats are naturally cautious around unfamiliar objects, a behaviour known as neophobia . A trap may contain attractive food, but if the perceived risk outweighs the reward, a rat may simply refuse to enter. Researchers and pest managers have traditionally tried to solve this problem by improving lures, making traps more appealing, or reducing fear of the trap itself. We explored a different possibility. Instead of changing the trap, could we change the rat’s perception of its options? An irresistible snack just out of reach To test this idea, we worked with wild black rats ( Rattus rattus ) in bushland around Sydney. We set up tracking tunnels which work much the same way as traps but the animals are free to leave. Outside some of the tunnel entrances, we placed a highly desirable peanut butter bait ball inside a steel mesh container. Rats could see and smell the peanut butter, but they couldn’t eat it. In effect, we created a “phantom decoy” – a tempting option that was present but unattainable. The idea was borrowed directly from behavioural economics. If the highly desirable but inaccessible food changed how rats perceived the available food inside the tunnel, rats might be more willing to enter. A surprising result The results were striking. Rats were 83% more likely to enter tunnels containing a basic food reward when the inaccessible “phantom” food was present. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that a “phantom decoy” effect, a phenomenon well documented in human decision-making , can be used to influence trap-entry behaviour in a wild mammal. The decoy itself could never be eaten. Yet its mere presence changed the rats’ decision-making behaviour. Importantly, our experimental controls showed that placing the same inaccessible food inside the tunnel didn’t increase entry rates, nor was the effect simply due to the extra food attracting more rats to the area. The increase in tunnel entry only happened when the inaccessible food was positioned outside the tunnel, suggesting it changed how rats evaluated the option of entering. This suggests rats weren’t simply responding to the amount of food available. Instead, their decisions were influenced by how the options were presented. While we can’t know exactly how a rat experiences these choices, the findings show that altering perceived alternatives can substantially influence how rats behave. What this could mean for pest control The practical implications are potentially significant. Pest managers often encounter animals that investigate traps or bait stations but refuse to enter. This problem occurs at every scale , from failed island eradications to backyard rats that seem impossible to catch. When lures alone aren’t enough to overcome an animal’s reluctance to enter, changing how it perceives its options may be an effective alternative. Our study suggests a relatively simple and inexpensive way to encourage animals to enter traps: add a highly desirable but inaccessible food option outside the trap entrance. Importantly, this approach doesn’t require a new trap design, sophisticated technology or costly equipment. It simply changes the decision-making environment. articles.description: Irina/Getty Images Have you ever wondered why restaurants include outrageously expensive bottles of wine on their menus? Often, those bottles aren’t expected to sell. Instead, they make the other wines seem better value even if they are still overpriced. By changing the context of the decision, the out-of-reach expensive option can nudge customers towards wanting the cheaper option more. Marketers use similar tricks all the time. A holiday package that’s sold out, a premium subscription nobody really wants, or a product that’s clearly overpriced can all influence how we perceive the alternatives around them. Behavioural economists call these influences “decoy effects” . They reveal that decisions are not always rational based on absolute value. Instead, they are often shaped by the options available at the time. Humans aren’t the only animals making decisions. Every day, wild animals weigh up risks and rewards: whether to investigate a novel object, where to forage, or whether entering a trap is worth the potential danger. That got us wondering: could a decoy influence a rat? That was the subject of our new study, published today in The Journal of Applied Ecology . The problem with trapping rats Rats are among the world’s most successful and adaptable animals. They damage crops and infrastructure, spread disease, threaten native wildlife and cost economies billions of dollars every year in damages and pest control. Despite more than a century of innovation and thousands of patented trap designs, trapping still depends on one crucial step: the animal must choose to enter the trap. This seemingly simple decision is often where pest control programs fail. Many rats are naturally cautious around unfamiliar objects, a behaviour known as neophobia . A trap may contain attractive food, but if the perceived risk outweighs the reward, a rat may simply refuse to enter. Researchers and pest managers have traditionally tried to solve this problem by improving lures, making traps more appealing, or reducing fear of the trap itself. We explored a different possibility. Instead of changing the trap, could we change the rat’s perception of its options? An irresistible snack just out of reach To test this idea, we worked with wild black rats ( Rattus rattus ) in bushland around Sydney. We set up tracking tunnels which work much the same way as traps but the animals are free to leave. Outside some of the tunnel entrances, we placed a highly desirable peanut butter bait ball inside a steel mesh container. Rats could see and smell the peanut butter, but they couldn’t eat it. In effect, we created a “phantom decoy” – a tempting option that was present but unattainable. The idea was borrowed directly from behavioural economics. If the highly desirable but inaccessible food changed how rats perceived the available food inside the tunnel, rats might be more willing to enter. A surprising result The results were striking. Rats were 83% more likely to enter tunnels containing a basic food reward when the inaccessible “phantom” food was present. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that a “phantom decoy” effect, a phenomenon well documented in human decision-making , can be used to influence trap-entry behaviour in a wild mammal. The decoy itself could never be eaten. Yet its mere presence changed the rats’ decision-making behaviour. Importantly, our experimental controls showed that placing the same inaccessible food inside the tunnel didn’t increase entry rates, nor was the effect simply due to the extra food attracting more rats to the area. The increase in tunnel entry only happened when the inaccessible food was positioned outside the tunnel, suggesting it changed how rats evaluated the option of entering. This suggests rats weren’t simply responding to the amount of food available. Instead, their decisions were influenced by how the options were presented. While we can’t know exactly how a rat experiences these choices, the findings show that altering perceived alternatives can substantially influence how rats behave. What this could mean for pest control The practical implications are potentially significant. Pest managers often encounter animals that investigate traps or bait stations but refuse to enter. This problem occurs at every scale , from failed island eradications to backyard rats that seem impossible to catch. When lures alone aren’t enough to overcome an animal’s reluctance to enter, changing how it perceives its options may be an effective alternative. Our study suggests a relatively simple and inexpensive way to encourage animals to enter traps: add a highly desirable but inaccessible food option outside the trap entrance. Importantly, this approach doesn’t require a new trap design, sophisticated technology or costly equipment. It simply changes the decision-making environment. Beyond rats The findings also raise a broader question. For decades, behavioural economists and psychologists have documented decision-making biases in humans. Increasingly, evidence suggests that some of these principles may extend beyond our own species. Animals, like humans, constantly make choices under uncertainty. Understanding those choices could unlock new ways to manage pest species , conserve threatened wildlife and improve animal monitoring. Sometimes, the best way to get an animal to choose option A may not be to make option A better. It may be to add option B. articles.content: He was the child star of the Osmonds who become a global celebrity by 14. Then, at 21, his career came crashing down. Here, he reveals how he survived his years in exile – and what happened when Jackson was accused of child abuse For a brief period in the early 1970s, Donny Osmond ruled the world. He was the global teenage heart-throb. Even Michael Jackson trailed behind him. He was 14 when his most famous song, Puppy Love, spent five weeks at No 1 in the UK. My sister had a huge poster of him on her bedroom wall. Then again, everybody’s sister had a poster of him on their bedroom wall. Between 1972 and 1973 he had six Top 5 hits in the UK, three of them No 1s (including The Twelfth of Never and Young Love). He was equally successful back home in the US. Osmond was clean-cut, religious and respectful, with a mighty ability to punch out cover versions of saccharine standards. From his purple velvet cap to his doleful eyes and dazzling all-American smile, he was a marketing dream. We’d only just finished with Beatlemania. And now there was Donnymania. Continue reading...

articles.content: ChiccoDodiFC / Getty Images On Friday, Turkish-American mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge announced he had produced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most important and famous open problems in mathematics, with the aid of an artificial intelligence (AI) model. Alpöge – a prominent figure in AI-assisted mathematics – announced the result via a four-page statement on his website . In it, he describes the Riemann hypothesis as “the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood”. He also notes that he wanted to publish earlier, but delayed because there was “a constraint to respect” – presumably commercial rules around Anthropic’s share market listing last week, which raised over US$100 billion. The claimed proof is the latest in a deluge of significant AI-assisted mathematical discoveries announced over the past six months, as AI companies turn their vast resources on one of humanity’s great intellectual activities as a testing ground. What is the Riemann hypothesis? First posed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis is about a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function (often written ζ( s )). This function is important in number theory because it is related to how prime numbers are distributed. It can be used to estimate how many prime numbers exist that are smaller than any given number. In essence, the Riemann hypothesis says that all “non-trivial” solutions of the equation ζ( s ) = 0 – the “zeroes” of the zeta function – must be on a particular vertical straight line. Alpöge’s proof actually claims to prove the broader claim known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis, likely first posed around 1884, which extends the idea to a bigger family of functions that are connected to many parts of number theory. Have people tried to prove it before? Over the past century and a half, there have been many attempts to prove the Riemann hypothesis and its generalisations. In 1900, German mathematician David Hilbert listed it in his influential collection of 23 problems for the 20th century. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute offered million-dollar prizes for solving seven key problems for the 21st century, and again a proof of the Riemann hypothesis was on the list. The hypothesis has been formulated in more than 100 equivalent ways . More than 12 trillion zeroes of the function have been checked and found to be on the critical line. But still, a proof that all the zeroes must be on that line has been elusive. Is this a better way to publish AI-assisted maths results? Over the past year, mathematicians have grown accustomed to AI companies releasing significant results in unceremonious dumps . Many high-profile discoveries have been announced with much fanfare. But behind the splashes have been seemingly unvetted and unedited AI-produced manuscripts. This offloads responsibility for actually checking the results onto the mathematical community, which has caused a great deal of discontent. Alpöge’s claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis has felt a little different. Instead, he has described part of his process working with a large language model as a collaborator. He outlines some of the ideas that make the proof work, and gives a timeline of how the key parts of the proof developed. The proof itself was published as more than 17 million lines of code in the mathematical formalisation software Lean, rather than in a human-readable form. Lean allows a proof to be written in a way that lets a computer check each step of the argument and verify it as correct. Alpöge’s justification for the Lean-only release was that “[t]he argument is incredibly long”. He said his attempts at an AI-produced explanation in English “hit 250,000+ pages”, and it was “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop’”. So is the proof correct? Does this mean the hypothesis has definitively been proven? Not quite. There may be problems with how a proof is formalised, and mathematicians generally agree that a Lean formalisation alone is not enough to confirm a proof. That said, Alpöge’s proof is looking good. The Lean Focused Research Organization and the MathLib community that develops and maintains Lean and its mathematical libraries released a joint statement stating their belief in the correctness of the proof. Canadian mathematician Daniel Litt described the odd situation in this way: (1) The Lean-formalized proof of the Riemann hypothesis is exceedingly likely to be correct. (2) No human understands it yet. What about human mathematicians? Hot on the heels of Alpöge’s claim was a hurried announcement by Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society. He released another proposed proof of the generalised Riemann hypothesis – this one by Stanford mathematician Alessandro Maria Masullo. Vakil characterised Masullo’s proof, presented in a 940-page manuscript entitled The Music of the Primes, as “all human, with no AI”. The proof was still being checked when it was released, and potential problems had been found within hours of publication. It remains to see whether these can be corrected. In Alpöge’s announcement, he was careful to give praise and credit to a variety of mathematicians and colleagues. This goes against a noticeable trend in which AI-written papers do little to cite earlier work. Alpöge also indicates he will endeavour “to understand and impart understanding of this argument and its certain simplifications, to speak about it, to write it properly”. In the coming years, this remarkable mathematical achievement will no doubt be discussed and dissected, and the proof made comprehensible to humans. This discovery may also provide one of the first good examples of how AI-assisted breakthroughs can be announced and shared in a way that respects the mathematical community. articles.content: COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey, arriving for the final plenary meeting. Mike Muzurakis/IISD/ENB , CC BY-SA After stretching almost two days overtime, the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed after countries failed to agree on an overarching deal to combat climate change. The breaking point was a draft text with no mention of a phase-out of fossil fuels. Nearly 40 countries, including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and vulnerable Pacific island nations such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands, formally objected to the final text. EU representatives called a climate deal that ignored phasing out fossil fuels “ unconscionable ”. But the summit also failed to deliver on several other significant issues. It was billed as the “implementation COP”, but delivered very few of the goals set by its co-presidents, Turkey and Australia. The rejection of the final text centred on other interrelated concerns : a lack of response to science that shows the world is about to breach 1.5°C of warming and inadequate financing for developing countries to respond to climate change. The aim was to triple adaptation financing to US$120 billion a year . That figure is now off the table, even though adaptation needs in the Global South alone are estimated at around US$500 billion a year . Talks about a just transition mechanism also made little progress. Even the goal for clean electricity to supply 35% of the world’s energy use by 2035 was only supported as a voluntary pledge by 90 countries. Science in the firing line I attended the summit in my role as chair of the World Climate Research Programme . My job, alongside other UN agencies, was to make sure the best available science underpinned the negotiations. It was disheartening to watch how hard that science was fought. The International Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) delivers its major reports every six or seven years and is currently working on its latest assessment. In between, the UN Environmental Programme’s ( UNEP ) annual Emissions Gap and Adaptation Gap reports and the World Meteorological Organization ’s State of the Global Climate report show how far off track nations are from meeting commitments made under the Paris Agreement. According to UNEP’s recent “overshoot” report and the 2026 Global Carbon Budget report , the world will reach 1.5°C of long-term warming around 2030. This breaches the lower limit of the Paris Agreement. For small island states and the least developed countries, the 1.5°C line is existential and non-negotiable. For the first time, COP31 discussed the concept of overshoot and how warming could be brought back down to 1.5°C again. This discussion split the room. Petrostates argued for carbon capture and removal, but at a scale that does not yet exist. Saudi Arabia, India and Russia, and at times China, discredited rigorously peer-reviewed findings. Small island states, meanwhile, refused any backsliding. Delay tactics Another flashpoint was an attempt to wave away the annual science reports altogether. Saudi Arabia, India and Russia objected to citing any findings other than the IPCC assessments, dismissing annual reports as “grey literature”. Meetings and press conferences were hastily convened, where I and other scientists behind these reports had to set out just how robust they are. The biggest fight of the summit was over the timing of the IPCC’s next major report, its Seventh Assessment Report . The above countries were accused of pushing for a delay until 2029. Read more: Why fossil fuel-producing countries are stalling this crucial climate report Dozens of European, African and Pacific nations want the report delivered earlier so it can inform the 2028 Global Stocktake when the world will measure its progress against the Paris Agreement goals. Pushing back the science until after the stocktake is a way of making sure the reckoning has nothing to measure against. The COP31 summit’s worth will be remembered for its outcome. Organisers will have to weigh the enormous cost and carbon footprint of flying in 92,000 people against the failure to agree on a final text. I cannot help asking whether these summits have had their day, and whether a new model is needed now. Climate change will not wait for the negotiators. If the system built to act on the science cannot even agree to hear it on time, we must find one that will. Tim Naish receives funding from the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment. He chairs the Joint Scientific Committee of the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) and attended COP31 on a World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) badge as a climate science expert.

articles.content: Liverpool thrashed 10-man Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday to climb to fourth in the Premier League. But the defeat left United 19th, only one point above bottom-placed Crystal Palace. There was no new manager bounce for Mauricio Pochettino, who saw Leny Yoro sent off in the eighth minute for a last-ditch foul on Alexander Isak. Pochettino accepted full responsibility for the loss, but claimed the dismissal was wrong and United should have had a penalty moments earlier for a Jérémy Jacquet challenge on Bryan Mbeumo. 'It was a desperate take,"' writes Andy Hunter at Anfield. Read the full match report here Continue reading...

articles.content: Get a better night’s sleep with monitoring and guidance from smartwatches, smart rings, smart bands and sleep earbuds The best sleep masks and best Bluetooth sleep masks Getting quality sleep is just as crucial as getting enough sleep. And how you feel in the morning only tells part of the story. Smartwatches, smart bands, smart rings and sleep earbuds can all help fill in the details: how long it took you to doze off, how long you spent in deep sleep, how restless you were, your resting heart rate, even if you have night-time breathing difficulties. Armed with this information, you can learn how your lifestyle affects your sleep. Maybe your after dinner cappuccino triggers a night of tossing and turning, or you’re more restful after evening workouts. As the wise GI Joe once said, knowing is half the battle. And the more you know about your sleep, the better chance you have of improving it. Continue reading...
