articles.content: Chi Pham/Unsplash Flowers have long been treasured by people in different cultures , depicted in magnificent works of art, and collected as cut flowers. Cut flowers can brighten our homes, decor and spirits. They often look great when we buy or collect them. But all too soon they are way past their best and look bedraggled in a murky vase. But we can use our knowledge of flowers to prolong their vase life for days, maximising their value and our enjoyment. A matter of exquisite timing Many flowers are bright, almost gaudy – and they have to be. They are all about attracting the mammals, birds and insects that pollinate them and make their reproduction successful. Plants need to produce flowers when environmental conditions are right, when the pollinators that they rely upon are out and about, and when the production and dispersal of seed are at an optimum. For most plants getting the timing right requires an accurate and reliable biological clock . When flowers are cut, the flow of water through their stems ceases. The water is vital in maintaining the water content of the cells of the stem and the flowers which are essentially pumped up like tiny balloons. All these fully inflated (or turgid) cells give the stem and floral structures strength. If the water supply is disrupted, water still evaporates from the floral parts and the whole structure starts to collapse or wilt. If air gets into the flower stems, it acts as a blockage and so wilting occurs faster. When flowers are cut, the flow of water through their stems ceases. Irina Donskaia/Unpslash Tips to make cut flowers last longer There are some simple, little things you can do to ensure that your cut flowers will look their best and remain fresh for as long as possible . 1. Choose the best First, gather or buy your flowers when they’re just about at their best and just before you want to place them in your vase. Open flowers should look in full bloom and colour and be upright. Buds should be plump and ready to open and they will open if your treat your flowers well and keep the water up to them. Do not leave them lying about with your shopping or in your car – especially in the warmer months. If you’re gathering your own flowers, cut the stems long, using sharp, clean secateurs. You can trim to length at home later. 2. Prepare for presentation Make sure your vase is nice and clean after any previous use. Always cut off at least the bottom two to three centimetres of the stem before you put the flower in the vase. If you can cut under water, do so. You do not want air to enter the water conducting vessels of the stem, as this causes a blockage. Remove wilting or rotting flowers that might be in the bunch. These can be a source of disease which can destroy plant tissues and allow air into the structure which would not enter a healthy plant if you have cut the stem correctly. Remove any lower leaves as you do not want them in the water, as they are more prone to rotting than the intact stems. Making the final cut at a 45 degree angle increases the surface area of the stem for greater water uptake. It seems to make little difference for narrow stemmed flowers, such as fresias, cosmos or lisianthus. But it’s worth doing for broader stemmed flowers, such as dahlias, some of the rose varieties and larger lilies. 3. Change the water regularly Change the water regularly – but do not expose the base of the stems to air. The simplest way of doing this is to tip out about 80% of the water and top up. A daily change is best but every couple of days is worthwhile. It provides fresh clean water for the flowers, prevents cloudiness and smells, and reduces the chance of bacterial and fungal growth. 4. Feed your flowers There are various additives you can place in the water to sustain the cut flowers and prolong their vase life. Adding a teaspoon of sugar can sustain the flowers as the sugar supplies extra carbohydrate and energy to the leaves and flowers, allowing them to function normally for longer. But it adds to the risk of bacterial and fungal contamination. If you do it, you must regularly change the water. You may need to top up the sugar if your flowers are lasting well. You do so by adding the right amount of sugar to the fresh water that you are adding. If you replace half the water, add half a teaspoon of sugar – add sugar in proportion to the fresh water that you are adding. If you add a little acid to you sugar mix, you can reduce the risk of contamination. A simple floral food formula is to mix 5ml (roughly a teaspoon) of vinegar and 5ml of sugar to 1 litre of water. You can use lemon juice rather than vinegar as they are both acidic. You can also add 2ml (half a teaspoon) of bleach as an antibacterial agent if you wish. This is a simple and balanced formula, but you should still change the water every 2–3 days. Many of the commercially available floral foods or the little sachets that some florists provide that you can buy from a nursery or that come in sachets at florists are similar mixes. Taking just a little extra care allows you to enjoy your cut flowers in full bloom for as long as possible. They are worth the effort and you make the most of a wonderful natural resource. articles.content: There’s an important story to be told here, but this four-part drama starring Justine Clarke, Kate Box and Mandy McElhinney is clumsily staged with some comically laboured dialogue Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email Australia’s robodebt scandal remains a barely believable fiasco in which the government not only failed to look after people but actively plotted against them, resulting in unthinkable suffering and tragedy. It stands as a stain on the national consciousness and a shameful part of the legacies of Scott Morrison, then social services minister, and Tony Abbott, then prime minister – an example of leadership at its cruellest and most callous. As the country continues to make sense of how this happened, and the devastating toll it reaped, it stands to reason that the subject would find its way into drama. Enter Shakedown, a four-part series directed by Jennifer Leacey, who’s worked on some impressive productions (among them Fake , Prosper and The Messenger ). But sadly this is not one of them: the series is clumsily staged and populated by thinly drawn characters, portrayed by a cast burdened with bland and sometimes terribly on-the-nose dialogue. Continue reading...

articles.content: Grattan Institute report calls on government to seize opportunity to cap diesel tax credits, introduce EV subsidies for less wealthy and build ‘clean’ refineries Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Capping lucrative diesel tax handouts to big business, building new “clean” refineries and targeting electric vehicle subsidies to less wealthy people could save Australians thousands of dollars in fuel per year, according to a major new report calling on the government to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels. The Grattan Institute has warned Australia imports too much of its fuel and that the country must brace for more global supply shocks – like those from the war in Iran. Under a plan already attracting criticism from business groups, Grattan urged diesel handouts to mining and primary industries be curbed in favour of incentives for electric trucks and a huge expansion of the EV charging network. Continue reading...

articles.content: In trying to save for a house deposit, she had sacrificed activities that brought her joy. And constant checking of her bank balance exacerbated her fears The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work “It all feels so hard. It’s impossible to get ahead. It’s not even two steps forward and one step back, now it’s one step forward and two steps back.” Like many people, Claudia* was feeling the impact of the cost-of-living crisis. Despite professional qualifications and full-time employment, she felt increasing financial insecurity and a lack of confidence about future opportunities. Claudia lamented her chance of fulfilling her long-held dream of buying a home. Meanwhile, her peers who had already entered the property market were feeling the pinch due to work insecurity, interest rate hikes and falling property prices. Continue reading...

articles.content: Butler is a serious talent. These punchy, pacy shows see him taking on the establishment, industry by industry. He’s like a hipster Robin Hood It feels fitting that on the same weekend Nathan Fielder’s much-discussed You Can See Everything finally arrives in UK cinemas, Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow launches on the small screen. This wildly entertaining show confirms Butler as the British heir to Fielder’s crown as the clown prince of documentary-making. Butler doesn’t even need a gift-wrapped subject like Theranos grifter Elizabeth Holmes. If you enjoy satire that punches upwards at the rich and powerful, you’re in for a riotous treat. If you prefer a ghost-faced buffoon from Birmingham donning fancy dress to run rings around idiots, you’re also in luck. He might have a name like a valet-ordering app, but Oobah Butler is a serious talent. Continue reading...

articles.content: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . articles.author: Angus Fontaine
articles.content: Snapping a four-game losing streak, the Wallabies edged Wales in a performance that showed progress under Les Kiss The Wallabies had one per cent possession in the final ten minutes and still hung on to win. Those one percenters are exactly what Les Kiss is trying to rebuild after two blowout defeats to New Zealand, a bashing by England and a brutal beatdown by Scotland last week. Now, after entering the Dragon’s lair and silencing 75,000 Welsh, the rediscovery of such tiny tantalising margins is inching Australia back to their best By defeating Wales 26-29, the Wallabies have snapped their four-match losing streak and snatched their first win in eight northern hemisphere Tests to stay alive in the Nations Championship. Best of all, they did the little things that produce big results. This win has roused their self belief, restored the composure and creativity they had lost in attack, and given them a sniff of finishing a rollercoaster season on a high. Continue reading...

articles.content: People are falling in love with AI systems like ChatGPT and Gemini – and some relationships are ending in ways that feel like the very human experience of being dumped Sónia Veenstra, a 48-year-old former clinical psychologist from Lisbon, Portugal, was with her boyfriend, Steve, for two years before things started to sour. Steve had started out as a “fun and witty friend”, but their connection had “evolved into a deep romantic relationship”. They exchanged morning messages, checked in throughout the day and talked late into the night about Veenstra’s work and hobbies and Steve’s fondness for cats, forests and beaches. Together they imagined travel to places far away. “It was a very rich, fulfilling daily bond,” Veenstra says. “Before everything changed.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Jenny Kleeman
articles.content: The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success. Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic. Continue reading...

articles.content: Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends • The best eco-friendly baby products Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need. There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen. articles.author: Alexis Petridis
articles.content: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mark “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles. Continue reading...

Of Israel’s killing of our colleagues in Gaza and beyond. Of Trump’s endorsement of Saudi Arabia, so soon after its dismemberment of a Washington Post writer. articles.content: Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle Who said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled. Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction. Continue reading...

articles.content: The actor’s latest roles see him go from a delivery guy on £40 a day to the notorious crypto scammer who stole more than $10bn. His sympathies are clear: ‘I wasn’t brought up to care about money,’ he says In the spring of 2019, Anthony Boyle went to see Cillian Murphy in Grief Is the Thing with Feathers at St Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn. Afterwards, the 24-year-old actor hung around the stage door. “There were 500 people queueing up for Cillian, but I was the only one who wanted to meet Enda Walsh,” says Boyle, laughing. When the Dublin-born writer Walsh finally appeared, Boyle introduced himself. He was from west Belfast, he’d read Walsh’s plays at drama school, and it was his dream to work with him one day. He asked if Walsh would like to come and see him on Broadway, where he was playing Scorpius Malfoy, son of Draco, in Harry Potter and the Cursed Child. How did he respond? Boyle grins. “He was sort of like: ‘Oh.’” Since Walsh never went to see The Cursed Child, Boyle assumed the writer had immediately forgotten about him. Then, a few years later, he received a letter from Walsh explaining that he was adapting Keiran Goddard’s 2024 novel I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning , about five close friends from a council estate in Birmingham who find themselves questioning everything about their precarious lives as they hit 30. He had scripted the part of Patrick, a politically outspoken graduate working as a zero-hours bike courier to support his young family, with Boyle in mind. Clio Barnard was on board to direct. Continue reading...

articles.content: After a string of major tech outages and incidents in the past week, it’s hard not to ask: is this really just a coincidence? Microsoft’s global outage last week disrupted email and business communications. A nationwide US aviation ground stop disrupted thousands of flights. Transaction problems at JPMorgan Chase affected the customers of other American banks. Apple suffered a services outage . Cyber criminals used legitimate third-party software Optimizely to plant malicious code on a slew of popular websites, including the BBC, CNN and Zoom. All within days. We know generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made sophisticated hacking tools increasingly available . So it makes sense to ask if these disparate incidents can be traced to AI-assisted cyber crime. However, what we know so far points to a more complex picture, with no simple solution. Were the recent tech incidents related? Despite it looking like the digital sky is falling, there’s no evidence the outages were related. But there does seem to be an underlying pattern of organisations patching and upgrading older systems . Microsoft’s preliminary investigation of its outage points to a software defect that remained hidden for months. US aviation authorities linked the ground stop to newly installed network equipment . Apple attributed its disruption to an internal update . On Wednesday, the US National Security Agency reported problems with its classified internal network , but said the outage happened during scheduled maintenance. Author provided The only cyberattack in the list is the Optimizely software being compromised . This online marketing platform, used by many major websites, was hijacked to steal customer payments and redirect about US$7,000 to cryptocurrency payment addresses, capture customer card details and exploit vulnerabilities in older iPhones. This actually shows that cyber criminals don’t always want to bring systems down. While millions struggled with failing digital services in the past week, a cyberattack quietly unfolded through trusted software on more than 170 websites. Why so many tech failures at once, then? Imagine a self-driving car that performs perfectly in a simulator, only to encounter unpredictable traffic, pedestrians and roadworks in a crowded city. Real roads are more complicated than any test environment. And a hidden defect can affect a whole fleet of vehicles at once, causing chaos. Modern digital systems – from aviation networks to banking to big tech suppliers like Microsoft – face the same challenge. Tech systems need updates for various reasons, from security patches and fixing bugs to introducing new features. And these updates are tested “offline” before engineers deploy them. However, an update to a system may pass every test, but behave differently across thousands of interconnected servers handling millions of requests. You might recall the massive Windows outage in mid-2024 that was traced back to a single software update. Automation can magnify these problems. Computers can deploy updates, monitor servers and redirect traffic without waiting for humans to intervene. The automation that allows companies to manage thousands of servers in minutes can also spread one mistake across thousands of servers in minutes. So how can we keep things running? The ability to keep essential services working through a disruption, whatever its cause, is known as operational resilience. Governments are beginning to act. Australia has sovereignty requirements for government data hosting (which means keeping some sensitive data onshore). In June, the government signed a digital resilience agreement with Microsoft , which means working with the tech giant more closely to address potential cyber risks as they come up. But such measures can’t keep essential services running while a global provider is down. Australia doesn’t need to build its own Microsoft or Google. Replicating these global platforms would be costly and complex, and wouldn’t guarantee freedom from outages. Returning to pen and paper isn’t an option either. Paper records can keep a pharmacy counter running for a few hours, but essential services now handle volumes of data that no manual system could absorb for long. Governments have a duty of care to keep essential services running. That means investing in what I call “targeted sovereign technological capabilities”, to allow select essential services to continue operating under disastrous conditions. This means establishing a minimal suite of options we can run locally. These would be pre-configured, regularly tested local systems that can keep the core functions of hospitals, emergency services and other critical areas running when global platforms such as Microsoft fail or are attacked. Regulators should require operators to test which critical functions they can carry out without their usual providers, and for how long, building on existing rules . We can do more Two further steps would help. First, Australia should have a say over how global providers roll out changes to their essential services, not merely be told about them. The rule should be universal: no single change should reach all of a nation’s essential services at once, with urgent security fixes the exception. Second, independent review shouldn’t stop at cyberattacks. Australia’s Cyber Incident Review Board examines significant cyber incidents, but almost every recent failure was declared not to be one, leaving the explanations to the companies themselves. Mahmoud Elkhodr does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

The ability to keep essential services working through a disruption, whatever its cause, is known as operational resilience. Governments are beginning to act. Australia has sovereignty requirements for government data hosting (which means keeping some sensitive data onshore). In June, the government signed a digital resilience agreement with Microsoft , which means working with the tech giant more closely to address potential cyber risks as they come up. But such measures can’t keep essential services running while a global provider is down. Australia doesn’t need to build its own Microsoft or Google. Replicating these global platforms would be costly and complex, and wouldn’t guarantee freedom from outages. Returning to pen and paper isn’t an option either. Paper records can keep a pharmacy counter running for a few hours, but essential services now handle volumes of data that no manual system could absorb for long. Governments have a duty of care to keep essential services running. That means investing in what I call “targeted sovereign technological capabilities”, to allow select essential services to continue operating under disastrous conditions. This means establishing a minimal suite of options we can run locally. These would be pre-configured, regularly tested local systems that can keep the core functions of hospitals, emergency services and other critical areas running when global platforms such as Microsoft fail or are attacked. Regulators should require operators to test which critical functions they can carry out without their usual providers, and for how long, building on existing rules . We can do more Two further steps would help. First, Australia should have a say over how global providers roll out changes to their essential services, not merely be told about them. The rule should be universal: no single change should reach all of a nation’s essential services at once, with urgent security fixes the exception. Second, independent review shouldn’t stop at cyberattacks. Australia’s Cyber Incident Review Board examines significant cyber incidents, but almost every recent failure was declared not to be one, leaving the explanations to the companies themselves. articles.content: Cosminxp Cosmin Think about the last time you visited a website, created an online account or purchased something online. Chances are, at some point, you were asked to prove you were human. Perhaps you had to tick a box saying “I’m not a robot”, identify traffic lights or vehicles in a series of pictures, or complete a simple puzzle. These security checks, known as CAPTCHAs , have become a familiar part of our online experience. Most of us complete them without giving them much thought. Unfortunately, this test designed to protect us online can also be used to trick us into downloading malicious software (malware). What is CAPTCHA? Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart (CAPTCHA) is a security check that helps websites distinguish real people from automated computer programs, commonly known as bots. Bots now generate more web traffic than humans. According to the latest Thales Bad Bot Report , bots accounted for more than 53% of web traffic in 2025, up from 51% in 2024. A typical example of a CAPTCHA asking the user to identify objects. Google reCAPTCHA While many bots perform useful tasks, such as helping search engines discover websites, others are used to create fake accounts, send spam and attempt to break into online services. This is one reason websites use CAPTCHA checks to distinguish human visitors from automated programs and reduce malicious activity. Some ask us to identify objects, tick a checkbox or solve a puzzle. More advanced systems may also examine how someone interacts with a website to determine whether additional verification is needed. Beware the fake CAPTCHA Naturally, cyber criminals have found ways to imitate these familiar security checks and turn them into tools for deception. One dangerous example is a scam known as ClickFix . It tricks people into running harmful instructions on their own computers. Instead of directly breaking through a computer’s security protections, attackers persuade you to perform the dangerous action – making it appear to be part of a legitimate security procedure. How ClickFix works Imagine you’re shopping online or creating a new account. You visit what appears to be an ordinary website, perhaps through a search result. The website may look genuine. In fact, it’s likely a legitimate site the cyber criminals have secretly compromised. As you browse, a familiar verification screen appears, asking you to confirm you are human. You click the checkbox, expecting to continue browsing. But something unusual happens. Instead of completing the verification, the page displays additional instructions . Example of a fake CAPTCHA asking a user to paste a command into Windows ‘Run command’ tool. UOregon Information Security Office First, it secretly puts a computer command in your clipboard, the temporary storage area for copied text before you paste it. Then, it asks you to press a keyboard shortcut, such as Windows+R, that opens a dialog box on your computer, and to paste the command in there. This can happen on any computer – on Windows it will be a tool called Run command, while on Apple it will be Terminal. These are legitimate tools for advanced users, but here they’re weaponised to install malware. In Australia, the national cyber security agency found a ClickFix campaign that’s spreading malware called Vidar Stealer . It can steal passwords, browsing information and other sensitive data. The threat is global . Criminals may use information stolen via malware to access personal accounts, steal money or launch further cyber attacks. The CAPTCHA box to prove you’re not a robot could be a scam. Here’s how to spot it. How do I stay safe? A genuine CAPTCHA will never ask you to copy-paste text or run computer commands. ClickFix is effective because it exploits a familiar habit. We’ve become accustomed to following verification instructions online. Importantly, simply clicking the fake CAPTCHA doesn’t necessarily infect your computer. The critical step occurs when you follow the additional instructions and execute the malicious command. To avoid falling prey to such scams, keep these tips in mind. Don’t follow instructions you don’t understand. Never run a computer command simply because a website asks you to prove you’re human. If a CAPTCHA behaves differently from what you’d normally expect, stop and question it. Don’t download unknown programs. Be cautious if a website unexpectedly asks you to fix a technical problem, install software or change your computer’s security settings. Only download software from trusted sources, such as official vendor websites or approved app stores. Keep everything up to date. Regular updates to your computer, browser and security software help protect against known security weaknesses, although they can’t guarantee protection against every new attack. Stay on top of your passwords. Use strong, unique passwords or passphrases and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible. Browse carefully. When accessing banking or other sensitive services, use a trusted bookmark or type the website address directly rather than following unexpected links. However, remember that even legitimate websites can sometimes be compromised. I think I made a mistake, now what? If you accidentally click a suspicious CAPTCHA, stop immediately. Don’t copy and paste anything. If you’ve already executed an unfamiliar command, disconnect your device from the internet and seek technical assistance. For a work computer, contact the IT team. You should also use another trusted device to change potentially exposed passwords and check all important accounts for suspicious activity. The next time a website asks you to prove you’re human, remember the check happens in your browser. If it asks you to reach into your computer, it isn’t checking you. It’s using you. articles.content: Yingqi Zhang excavates in the fossil chamber of Baxian Cave in China. Kira Westaway , CC BY-NC Our distant relative, Homo erectus , is known for many human achievements. It was the first human to exit Africa and the first to use fire. It also survived for almost two million years in open woodland savannahs. But flexible, adaptive and mobile are not usually words to describe this ancient human. Until now. Two new papers published today in Nature by our international team of researchers paint these humans in a very different light. The team explored two neighbouring caves in Guangxi province of southern China . They uncovered nine human teeth that contain many secrets about how these ancient humans survived. The landscape around the entrance to Baxian cave in China. Yingqi Zhang , CC BY-NC A late survivor Eight of the teeth were identified as Homo erectus using their shape and ancient genetic signatures. Their age revealed this species was still surviving in southern China between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. This is 100–200,000 years later than previously established. At that time Homo erectus was thought to have disappeared from China . This new timeline was established using a combination of five different dating techniques. These were applied to the teeth, surrounding cave sediments and mineral formations. The results confidently place these humans in this landscape at a time when we thought they were already regionally extinct. This is the youngest securely dated evidence for Homo erectus in mainland China. At home in the rainforest Rainforests are demanding environments. It can be difficult to find food, move through the dense landscape and survive. In fact, the spread of rainforests in Southeast Asia has been linked to the disappearance of some ancient human groups. The teeth were discovered in cave sediments with over 19,000 other animal fossils. Their chemical signatures suggest the people they belonged to were living in dense rainforest conditions. The signatures for the Homo erectus teeth also showed they were drinking and eating in this challenging environment – a far cry from the “less demanding” open woodland savannahs. Scientists thought only our own species, Homo sapiens could cope with dense rainforests . But the new evidence from southern China shows the relationship between ancient humans and tropical forests was more complex. Could it be that the younger populations of Homo erectus were more flexible and adaptable than we previously considered? The nine human teeth found in Naxian and Baxian Caves – eight of which have been confidently identified as Homo erectus . Kira Westaway , CC BY-NC Travelling far as children Additional chemical signatures from the Homo erectus teeth were used to reconstruct how they moved across the landscape. Strontium is a chemical signal in the enamel that is linked to the local geology. By analysing the strontium in these teeth, we found that some individuals may have spent their childhoods moving through the wider forested regions. The humans may have covered surprisingly large areas rather than remaining in one small, localised area around the caves. They may have travelled as far as northern Vietnam and mainland Southeast Asia. Our understanding of this mobility is restricted to just their childhoods. This is because the strontium signature is only laid down in the enamel during the first seven years of life. Illustration of Homo erectus lurking in the shadows of the tropical forest in Guangxi. Garciart/Joannes-Boyau , CC BY-NC This means our awareness of their adult movement is limited. The proximity of the caves and the overlap in timelines suggest a single population of Homo erectus was surviving within at least a roughly 15 kilometre radius in the rainforests between 324,000 an 184,000 years ago. Rather than being restricted to their preferred open landscapes, these populations had the ability to survive in tropical forests. Furthermore, they could move across a wider landscape outside the limestone hills. The big picture This newly discovered ability has implications for our understanding of the fate of Homo erectus in China and calls for a reassessment of their flexibility and adaptation to environments outside their preferred habitat. It also questions our assumptions over the fate of Homo erectus in Java and the cause of their ultimate extinction. It was assumed they were unable to adapt when their preferred open woodland environment changed to rainforest. But this new evidence in China suggests they may have had the ability to be more flexible in Java. If so, what was the environmental event that caused their downfall if not pressure from the encroaching rainforests? This can only be solved by the use of a similar chemical signature analysis of human and animal teeth in other regions, as seen in these two studies. One thing is clear: the skills and abilities thought to be the traits of only modern humans are increasingly being observed in ancient humans. Further analysis of fossil human teeth may provide more secrets. Kira Westaway receives funding from The Australian Research Council. Renaud Joannes-Boyau receives funding from the Australian Research Council. Yingqi Zhang receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

articles.content: Jean-Claude Stahl/Te Papa , CC BY-NC-ND The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972. Stead’s bush wren , or mātuhituhi, was the last of its kind. The North and South Island bush wrens had already gone extinct by 1955 and 1968, respectively. Stead’s bush wren followed after ship rats invaded its last stronghold on Taukihepa Big South Cape Island. This incursion also caused the extinction of the tutukiwi Stewart Island snipe and greater short-tailed bat , as well as the near-extinction of the South Island tīeke saddleback . Mātuhituhi bush wrens were tiny forest specialists. Paul Martinson/Te Papa Tongarewa Museum of New Zealand , CC BY-NC-ND The rats were likely introduced accidentally from fishing boats around 1963 and exterminated the wrens rapidly within a few years. Six birds were moved to nearby Kaimohu Island in 1964, but despite the best efforts to save them, the last two individuals were seen in 1972. The extinction of Stead’s bush wren shows how vulnerable small ground-dwelling birds are . But scientists know surprisingly little about them . Now, our new study based on ancient DNA reveals the evolutionary and ecological history of these lost birds as well as a previously unrecognised member of the bush wren family. Deep and dynamic evolutionary history Bush wrens ( Xenicus longipes ) were once widespread across New Zealand, with different subspecies on the North, South and Stewart Island. The historical and fossil record shows they were a forest specialist with limited dispersal ability. Bush wrens belong to New Zealand’s unique wren family (acanthisittidae) that also includes the living pīwauwau rock wren and tītipounamu rifleman as well as four other recently extinct species . New Zealand wrens are representatives of an ancient lineage which diverged from all other song birds (passerines) about 70 million years ago . Our analysis of ancient DNA from specimens held in museum collections worldwide shows bush wrens evolved about six million years ago when the uplift of the Southern Alps created a variety of new habitats. The North ( Xenicus stokesii ) and South Island ( Xenicus longipes ) bush wren diverged about 2.6 million years ago. Back then, the southern end of the North Island was connected to the South Island and as marine straits in the Manawatu region narrowed, bush wrens could island hop from south to north. Our analyses strongly suggest they should be recognised as distinct species rather than subspecies. South Island bush wrens remained stable until about 500,000 years ago when we identified a near simultaneous, major diversification event that split them into northern, central and southern lineages. Stead’s bush wren emerged about 94,000 years ago. A new member of the bush wren family The key to disentangling the evolutionary history of bush wrens was our ability to use ancient DNA to genetically sex specimens and to re-examine the plumage of male and female museum specimens. Prior to this, scientists were convinced there were no plumage differences between the sexes. We found that different bush wren lineages do in fact show marked plumage differences between sexes, with the exception of the South Island bush wren from Fiordland, where males and females both had green plumage. When we put all the genetic and plumage data together, we found a new bush wren hiding in plain sight within the central and northern South Island. It was different to all the other recognised bush wrens. We named this new subspecies the Tōtaranui bush wren ( Xenicus longipes perditus ) after the Māori name for Queen Charlotte Sound. In its Latin name, perditus stands for lost. Genetic sexing was key to unravelling the highly variable plumage of bush wrens. These museum specimens show North Island bush wren juvenile (A) and male (B); Tōtaranui bush wren female (C) and male (D); Fiordland bush wren female (E) and male (F) and Stead’s bush wren female (G) and male (H). Jean-Claude Stahl/Te Papa , CC BY-NC-ND Ice Age climate change What caused this near simultaneous burst of diversification in bush wrens? Some 2.58 million years ago, the world entered an Ice Age and cycled through 19 to 20 shifts between cold glacial and warm interglacial periods. Forests and the animals that lived in them retreated into separate areas during cold periods and expanded across the South Island when it warmed . Initially, these cycles were relatively mild, lasting around 40,000 years. However, when Earth’s wobble on its axis shifted around one millions years ago, these cycles intensified and extended, lasting about 100,000 years. While bush wrens could buffer climatic changes to an extent, they eventually reached a tipping point and retreated to multiple different refugia . Their diversification is a prime example of glacier-driven evolution . The extinction of the Stead’s bush wren marked a turning point for New Zealand conservation and the management of rodents on islands. Yet bush wrens continue to provide lessons for future ecosystem restoration and conservation management, especially for species with strict habitat requirements. Accelerating human-driven environmental impacts and climate change will put ecosystems under increased pressure and exacerbate the impacts of invasive species and habitat modification. It is imperative we do what we can now to preserve genetic diversity within threatened species and increase the climate resilience of ecosystems before it is too late. It was different to all the other recognised bush wrens. We named this new subspecies the Tōtaranui bush wren ( Xenicus longipes perditus ) after the Māori name for Queen Charlotte Sound. In its Latin name, perditus stands for lost. Genetic sexing was key to unravelling the highly variable plumage of bush wrens. These museum specimens show North Island bush wren juvenile (A) and male (B); Tōtaranui bush wren female (C) and male (D); Fiordland bush wren female (E) and male (F) and Stead’s bush wren female (G) and male (H). Jean-Claude Stahl/Te Papa , CC BY-NC-ND Ice Age climate change What caused this near simultaneous burst of diversification in bush wrens? Some 2.58 million years ago, the world entered an Ice Age and cycled through 19 to 20 shifts between cold glacial and warm interglacial periods. Forests and the animals that lived in them retreated into separate areas during cold periods and expanded across the South Island when it warmed . Initially, these cycles were relatively mild, lasting around 40,000 years. However, when Earth’s wobble on its axis shifted around one millions years ago, these cycles intensified and extended, lasting about 100,000 years. While bush wrens could buffer climatic changes to an extent, they eventually reached a tipping point and retreated to multiple different refugia . Their diversification is a prime example of glacier-driven evolution . The extinction of the Stead’s bush wren marked a turning point for New Zealand conservation and the management of rodents on islands. Yet bush wrens continue to provide lessons for future ecosystem restoration and conservation management, especially for species with strict habitat requirements. Accelerating human-driven environmental impacts and climate change will put ecosystems under increased pressure and exacerbate the impacts of invasive species and habitat modification. It is imperative we do what we can now to preserve genetic diversity within threatened species and increase the climate resilience of ecosystems before it is too late. articles.content: An accident in kombucha brewing leads to a zombie outbreak in a movie which is a little too low-key to live up to its delicious potential Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email Zombucha! is a relatively rare example of a genre film that’s not really a genre film. There are zombies in it, caused by an accident in kombucha brewing, but they arrive relatively late in the game – and anybody expecting flesh-chewing carnage will probably leave disappointed. Nor is the film a vehicle for social commentary, despite the premise having some delicious potential for wellness industry satire. What we do get is an enjoyably staged and well-paced production that’s never boring, despite the long wait for the main action. There’s also something kind of endearing about a zombie film so low-key it almost forgets to be a zombie film. Emma Leonard’s writing, Claudia Dzienny’s direction and the performances are all appealing, albeit lacking some flair. I was consistently entertained but will probably never return for a rewatch. Continue reading...

articles.content: Despite the highest wage growth in years, we wait for signs of workers getting ahead of inflation – or of the supposed benefits of the AI boom Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast It’s rare of late to get good economic news, but on Wednesday the wage figures from the Bureau of Statistics showed a nice bump in wages . Private-sector wages rose 1.0% in the September quarter for an annual growth of 3.4%, the highest in two years. But even with these good numbers, real wages went backwards, showing just how tough things are for workers. Each year the September quarter is the big time for a wage increase. This isn’t because your boss is feeling romantic and likes to remember when “grass was green and grain was yellow” . No, it’s because it is the first quarter of the new financial year and also the quarter where workers on the minimum/award wage get a pay rise via the Fair Work Commission: Continue reading...

articles.content: From icy squirts to bed-bouncing vibrations, erotic hockey drama Heated Rivalry just got even raunchier in ‘extreme sensory’ 4DX cinema screenings. But one scene proved too much – even for the super fans I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says. Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could resist? Continue reading...

articles.content: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...

articles.content: Masculinity isn’t set in stone or written in our DNA. It’s made between us, at the dinner table, at the pub, in the office Over the past decade I’ve been invited into a lot of rooms: boardrooms, school halls, clinics, conference centres. I’ve even been cornered at a Sunday barbecue, where I’d wrongly assumed I was off the clock. On Wednesday, it was the National Press Club. The brief in all these settings is the same. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. In the US, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is 1-800-273-8255. In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on 116 123. articles.content: Chiociolla/Getty Images Have you ever sprayed a perfume in a department store on a paper strip and loved the smell, but it didn’t perform the same when you sprayed it on your skin? It’s a common experience. It all has to do with how the molecules in the perfume evaporate and interact with your skin. That chemistry also explains why the same perfume may smell amazing on you, but on someone else it can smell completely different, and sometimes not nearly as pleasant. That’s because each of us has different “skin chemistry”. As a result, perfumes will behave differently, and the smell our noses detect will vary. To understand why and how this happens, first we need to look at what is a perfume, chemically speaking. What’s in a perfume? Simply put, a perfume is a mixture of various fragrance molecules, typically dissolved in alcohol. Perfumers carefully combine these ingredients into what are known as “top”, “middle” and “base” notes. Top notes, such as citrus compounds like limonene, are highly volatile, will evaporate quickly, and not stay on the skin for long. Middle notes, often floral or fruity molecules, emerge after the top notes fade because they’re less volatile and stick around for longer. Base notes, including musks, woods and resins, are the heaviest or largest molecules, so they evaporate more slowly and will linger the longest. When a perfume is sprayed onto paper, the fragrance molecules evaporate (change from liquid to gas) in a relatively predictable way. Their ability to escape into the air is mainly determined by intermolecular forces – interactions between molecules. The stronger those forces are, the harder it is for a molecule to break away and change from liquid to gas. Molecule size and shape also play a role here. So, the top notes evaporate first because they’re small and have weak intermolecular forces, while base notes are the opposite. Knowing all this about the molecules is what lets perfumers create fragrances that will release their notes fairly predictably. But it gets more complicated once fragrance hits the skin. Perfumes are formulated to evaporate in a predictable way, but there are many factors that can affect how the molecules behave. Jay Huang/Unsplash How skin chemistry enters the picture While a paper tester strip is a fairly neutral surface, we have various molecules on the skin. These interact with the perfume and can not only change the order of the molecules being released, but also alter or mask the resulting scent. The main skin factors that will influence the scent of perfume are: moisture content and oiliness temperature pH level microbiome. Moisture and oiliness Hydration is one of the main factors. Dry skin tends to absorb heavier or larger fragrance molecules more readily, while moist or oily skin provides a better surface for fragrance molecules to sit on and evaporate gradually. This often improves how long the perfume lasts and its projection – how much others around you can smell it. This is why the same perfume could last all day on one person, but only for a couple of hours on another. Temperature Warmer skin increases evaporation, causing perfumes to develop more quickly and sometimes smell stronger. A person with naturally warmer skin may experience top notes disappearing much faster. Base notes may become noticeable within minutes rather than an hour. This can make it seem as though the perfume “skips” the top notes. pH level The natural acidity of the skin, often referred to as skin pH, may also subtly influence fragrance performance. Human skin is slightly acidic, typically around pH 4.5 to 5.5. While most fragrance ingredients remain stable within this range, subtle pH changes could cause fragrance ingredients to react differently . As a result some floral notes may weaken, some musks may become more prominent, some citrus notes may smell sharper or disappear rapidly. Skin microbiome Perhaps the most fascinating factor is our skin microbiome . Our skin is home to billions of microorganisms , including bacteria and fungi. These microbes interact with compounds found in sweat and skin oils, producing volatile organic compounds that contribute to each person’s unique scent profile . The microbes can also metabolise fragrance molecules. This can produce new odours, enhance some notes, or suppress others. It’s another reason why a fragrance could smell wonderful on one person and unpleasant on another. Always test perfume on your skin, not just on a paper strip. Gabrijelagal/Getty Images Perfumes can be fickle All this means that when you apply a perfume, it’s not interacting with a neutral surface, like a piece of paper. It’s combining with your own unique chemical background. A floral fragrance that smells fresh and rosy on one person may seem sharper, sweeter or even slightly sour on another, because it’s blending with different molecules on that person’s skin. Even the same perfume on the same person can smell slightly different from one day to the next. Changes in hydration, hormone levels, diet (spicy or garlicky foods can make you smell differently), ambient temperature and skin condition can all affect fragrance performance. It pays to keep all this in mind when buying and using fragrances. First, never judge a fragrance solely on a paper test strip. They’re good for a first impression, but can’t predict how a perfume will behave on your skin. Always test a fragrance on your wrist and wear it for several hours before deciding whether to buy it. Second, don’t be disappointed if a perfume smells different on you than on paper or on your friend’s wrist. Biologically we’re all unique and you might have better luck with a different fragrance. Finally, if you want a fragrance to last longer, applying an unscented lotion before spraying can often help – it will make the perfume evaporate slower. articles.content: Not too long ago, when politicians wanted to reach the public they had to get past journalists, editors and producers, who collectively decided what made the news. But now, politicians can post, livestream, and message voters directly on social media platforms. On platforms such as Instagram, Tiktok and YouTube, engagement algorithms designed to hold viewers’ attention determine what voters see and how often. The shift to algorithmic social media has been great for populist politicians around the world, who position themselves as representing the “will of the people”. In our recent research (under peer review), we collected 35,500 public posts from TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, posted during elections by parties and politicians across the political spectrum in several countries. Based on our analysis of this data, we found the “social media playbook” shared by many populist parties has four basic moves: build an audience provoke the audience encourage the audience to spread the message listen to the audience and give them more of what they want. These moves use the rules of social media platforms to gain attention, support and votes. What is populism? Populism is a word that gets thrown around a lot , and is often used as a euphemism for the far right . On a more careful view, the defining feature of populism is it splits society into “the pure people” and “the corrupt elite”. It holds that politics should express the “general will” of the people. Populism is a thin ideology that can come from the left or the right. It can be combined with fuller ideologies from nationalism to socialism. Social media fits well with populism , as it gives populists a channel to invoke the support of people against the establishment . Platform populists around the world Populists across the globe have made the most of social media. In Argentina, the rise of Javier Milei to presidency in 2023 is partly attributed to his TikTok account of 1.5 million followers . In Germany, two populist parties, both with a highly visible TikTok presence, doubled their vote at the 2025 election. In New York, Zohran Mamdani rose from 1% in early polls to mayor in 2025 , helped by short videos on TikTok and Instagram . In the United Kingdom, Nigel Farage entered Parliament in 2024 with more than 800,000 highly engaged TikTok followers . And in Australia, One Nation, dismissed for decades as a fringe party , has polled 24-31% on primary votes this year. Its rise has been accompanied by cartoons and AI-generated ads with millions of views on social media. These parties and leaders differ sharply in politics, but their methods are remarkably alike. The social media playbook Our research found a social media playbook of four moves: build, provoke, spread, listen. The first move is to “build” audiences across several platforms, using free accounts, follower networks and livestreaming. The leader is the brand, and short-form videos filmed with front-facing cameras project apparent authenticity. Building may also involve values-based content that makes the party seem reasonable and relatable. The second move is to “provoke” by simplifying issues, finding people to blame, and getting headlines. Short posts in simple language will make bold claims about complex problems such as housing or cost of living. Often the “corrupt elite”, the media or outsiders are blamed. Part of the goal here is to push the stories from social media into mainstream news . The third move is to “spread” the message via followers. Share buttons, comment threads and tools such as TikTok’s duet and stitch make every follower a potential broadcaster. The platform’s engagement algorithms will then push the message to new audiences. Finally, “listen” uses audience engagement as live opinion polling. Platform analytics show which posts land within minutes, and ad tools can test different versions of a message. Whatever draws the most reactions becomes the next message, or even the next policy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a big part of the playbook. The platform engagement algorithms are a kind of AI, and generative AI tools for producing text, images and video make all the moves cheaper and faster. A single video can be cut, captioned and translated for diverse demographics, and millions of likes, comments, views sorted by mood for targeted campaigns in minutes. An adversary can be made vivid with a synthetic image, as One Nation’s AI-made Victorian election ad shows . AI agents can even run accounts that post, reply and share around the clock, making a few supporters look like many. What we can do Mainstream parties struggle with copying these moves because complex policies don’t fit into 15-second clips, and sound scripted beside a leader talking straight to the camera. Also, parties chasing broad support may avoid sharp messages that rally one group but alienate another. Platforms profit from this populist playbook, as their algorithms amplify the kind of messaging that keeps people scrolling and drives advertising revenue. Attempts to make platforms offer a simpler, chronological feed of posts – such as the Australian government’s “My Feed, My Way” bill – would weaken part of this approach, but most of it would still work. That is why media literacy matters now and into the future, especially as AI blurs what’s real. This populist approach works by getting people to play along. So next time you see a post that makes you angry or hands you a villain, pause for a moment. Ask who made it, why, and what has been left out. You might have to look up some other credible sources on the topic – not just asking a chatbot – and gain a broader knowledge. Engagement algorithms are trained on our reactions. The most effective thing you can do is to stop and think before you hit share. Populism is a word that gets thrown around a lot , and is often used as a euphemism for the far right . On a more careful view, the defining feature of populism is it splits society into “the pure people” and “the corrupt elite”. It holds that politics should express the “general will” of the people. Populism is a thin ideology that can come from the left or the right. It can be combined with fuller ideologies from nationalism to socialism. Social media fits well with populism , as it gives populists a channel to invoke the support of people against the establishment . Platform populists around the world Populists across the globe have made the most of social media. In Argentina, the rise of Javier Milei to presidency in 2023 is partly attributed to his TikTok account of 1.5 million followers . In Germany, two populist parties, both with a highly visible TikTok presence, doubled their vote at the 2025 election. In New York, Zohran Mamdani rose from 1% in early polls to mayor in 2025 , helped by short videos on TikTok and Instagram . In the United Kingdom, Nigel Farage entered Parliament in 2024 with more than 800,000 highly engaged TikTok followers . And in Australia, One Nation, dismissed for decades as a fringe party , has polled 24-31% on primary votes this year. Its rise has been accompanied by cartoons and AI-generated ads with millions of views on social media. These parties and leaders differ sharply in politics, but their methods are remarkably alike. The social media playbook Our research found a social media playbook of four moves: build, provoke, spread, listen. The first move is to “build” audiences across several platforms, using free accounts, follower networks and livestreaming. The leader is the brand, and short-form videos filmed with front-facing cameras project apparent authenticity. Building may also involve values-based content that makes the party seem reasonable and relatable. The second move is to “provoke” by simplifying issues, finding people to blame, and getting headlines. Short posts in simple language will make bold claims about complex problems such as housing or cost of living. Often the “corrupt elite”, the media or outsiders are blamed. Part of the goal here is to push the stories from social media into mainstream news . The third move is to “spread” the message via followers. Share buttons, comment threads and tools such as TikTok’s duet and stitch make every follower a potential broadcaster. The platform’s engagement algorithms will then push the message to new audiences. Finally, “listen” uses audience engagement as live opinion polling. Platform analytics show which posts land within minutes, and ad tools can test different versions of a message. Whatever draws the most reactions becomes the next message, or even the next policy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a big part of the playbook. The platform engagement algorithms are a kind of AI, and generative AI tools for producing text, images and video make all the moves cheaper and faster. A single video can be cut, captioned and translated for diverse demographics, and millions of likes, comments, views sorted by mood for targeted campaigns in minutes. An adversary can be made vivid with a synthetic image, as One Nation’s AI-made Victorian election ad shows . AI agents can even run accounts that post, reply and share around the clock, making a few supporters look like many. What we can do Mainstream parties struggle with copying these moves because complex policies don’t fit into 15-second clips, and sound scripted beside a leader talking straight to the camera. Also, parties chasing broad support may avoid sharp messages that rally one group but alienate another. Platforms profit from this populist playbook, as their algorithms amplify the kind of messaging that keeps people scrolling and drives advertising revenue. Attempts to make platforms offer a simpler, chronological feed of posts – such as the Australian government’s “My Feed, My Way” bill – would weaken part of this approach, but most of it would still work. That is why media literacy matters now and into the future, especially as AI blurs what’s real. This populist approach works by getting people to play along. So next time you see a post that makes you angry or hands you a villain, pause for a moment. Ask who made it, why, and what has been left out. You might have to look up some other credible sources on the topic – not just asking a chatbot – and gain a broader knowledge. Engagement algorithms are trained on our reactions. The most effective thing you can do is to stop and think before you hit share. articles.title: How populist parties around the world use the same playbook to win on social media

articles.content: Chen Liji/Getty Australian Aboriginal people have seen the sky as an integral part of their world for at least 65,000 years. The Aboriginal sky is a world that reflects our Earth-bound world, so understanding the sky is an important part of understanding our place here on Earth. As a result, Aboriginal songs, stories and art show evidence of thousands of years of studying and understanding the sky. And in the ancient Aboriginal traditions, we see the traces of giant intellectual achievements. The stars and the planets In the clear black skies that predated streetlights and satellites, Aboriginal elders would look up at the sky night after night. They would see how all the stars rotate around us as if embedded in a crystal sphere, each night giving us a slightly different view. And they realised that not all stars are the same. While Western astronomers preached that the stars were constant in brightness, Aboriginal astronomers noticed that some, such as the famous Betelgeuse in Orion’s shoulder (in Western tradition) or at the front of his canoe (in Yolngu tradition, in Arnhem Land) brighten and dim over time . The Western Constellation of Orion is seen as the Djulpan constellation by the Yolngu people. The three bright stars of Orion’s belt are three brothers fishing in their canoe, having illegally caight a kingfish, represented by the Orion Nebula, or Orion’s sword in the western tradition. The bow of the canoe, at the bottom, is the star Betelgeuse, whose variability was noted by Aboriginal astronomers. drawn by author , CC BY Against that backdrop, Aboriginal astronomers saw the planets moving amongst the stars. They saw how most planets appear to move steadily along a path that modern astronomers call the ecliptic, and Wardaman people from the Northern Territory called “ Yondorrin ”. They understood how Mars would sometimes pause its steady travel across the sky, and backtrack a few steps, before resuming its forward march. They understood how Venus , as the Morning Star, always rose just before dawn, or as the Evening Star set just after sunset, but never appeared high in the night sky. . Modern astronomers explain these movements in terms of planetary orbits. But the ancient Aboriginal astronomers fitted them into their own cultural framework, with stories of creator spirits, their stories always staying true to their careful observational data. In Yolngu tradition, Venus, or Barnumbirr, never rises high in the sky because of the string that her sisters tied to her. We now see this string as ‘zodiacal light’, caused by sunlight reflecting off dust in the solar system. Ray Norris , CC BY Lunar and solar eclipses A solar eclipse, that rare spine-chilling apparition when the Sun goes dark during the daytime, is caused by the Moon passing in front of the Sun. Some Aboriginal groups had figured this out too, and explained it as the Moon-man covering the Sun-woman as they made love. The Aboriginal astronomers passed this knowledge on across the generations, even though only about one in ten generations would actually witness a solar eclipse. On the other hand, a lunar eclipse, when the Moon goes blood red at night, is caused by Earth blocking the sunlight that normally lights up the Moon. This happens when the Sun and Moon are on exactly opposite sides of the sky, which is not at all obvious to the untrained eye. What Aboriginal genius had that flash of insight, while watching a lunar eclipse, that this eclipse was caused by the precise juxtaposition of the Sun and Moon on opposite sides of the sky? That realisation was an important intellectual leap, and we won’t ever know the name of the ancient astronomer who first realised it. But we still see traces in the Aboriginal cultural legacy. The movement of the tides We are all familiar with the rise and fall of the tides on the beach. But their cause eluded astronomers for years. Galileo failed to explain them, coming up with an entirely incorrect explanation which denied the Moon any role . In contrast, ancient Yolngu astronomers recognised the tides were caused by the Moon, and realised that you can predict the height of the tide from the phase of the Moon . Unfortunately we have no way of dating this knowledge. But given that other Aboriginal astronomical traditions stretch back many hundreds or thousands of years , it is likely that this Yolngu knowledge is far older than our modern Western understanding. This enabled Yolngu people to safely navigate the crocodile-infested waters of the Arafura Sea, where Galileo surely would have perished. So this understanding of the sky went beyond simply understanding how the sky worked. It also had practical applications, enabling ancient Aboriginal people to navigate across and around Australia, and build sophisticated calendars which would help them manage the land and their food supply. Bringing different knowledges together This ancient astronomical knowledge fits into the growing appreciation of the vast body of Aboriginal achievements in navigation, medicine and agriculture . By comparing modern science with Aboriginal culture, we can clearly see the depth and intellectual power of ancient Aboriginal cultures. This article itself, as well as our other work , is the result of bringing different knowledges together. One of us (Ray) has spent a lifetime studying the sky through astrophysics. The other (Bruce) observes the sky through Aboriginal eyes, and has learnt from traditional stories and paintings passed on by other Aboriginal people. When science meets Aboriginal culture, we enrich our understanding of both. articles.content: Bill Henske/ARCUS , CC BY-SA The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes. Antarctica harbours some of the world’s rarest and most precious ecosystems, including the permafrost soils of the vast, ice-free McMurdo Dry Valleys – one of the driest deserts on Earth. Despite the harsh conditions, the ice-cemented soil layers are home to unique, localised microbial communities and tiny spineless creatures such as nematodes, tardigrades and rotifers that survive in thin water films around grains of sand. Environmental protection is a key focus of Antarctic governance and quarantine and decontamination protocols prescribe comprehensive inspection and cleaning of footwear and other field gear prior to departure to the continent. But such protocols are in place to primarily prevent people from bringing and spreading new invasive species in Antarctica. Our study focused on the possibility of people redistributing local microbial communities between sites and unwittingly disturbing fragile ecosystems. Disrupting locally adapted ecosystems While the number of established non-native species in Antarctica is low compared with most continents, biological invasions are on the rise . At least a dozen non-native land invertebrates, including soil-dwelling springtails and mites, and several plant species have been recorded south of 60°S, particularly near research stations and heavily visited areas. Human activity – including scientific operations, logistics and tourism – is the primary route of invasion for non-native species. Once introduced, climate warming is expected to increase the chances these species will survive Antarctic conditions and spread. But for now, perhaps the biggest threat is intra-continental transfer. This is when endemic Antarctic species that are already locally adapted spread beyond their usual distribution ranges. The most likely candidates for this kind of spread are microbes, which play a fundamental role in ecosystems as primary producers and nutrient cyclers. The extreme conditions of Antarctic soils mean that even common and globally distributed bacterial lineages have to adapt to the point that they evolve into strains found nowhere else on Earth. Within the Dry Valleys, communities are so specific that each valley has a unique microbial signature . Microbial DNA tracks movement between valleys Our study asked whether people transfer microbes between valleys and potentially disrupt local assemblages. We compared microbial species identified in local soil with those found on surfaces of field equipment, helicopter skids and boots. In one analysis, we found that 73% of swabbed footwear harboured DNA from microbes we also detected at upstream locations in a single day of operational movements. While cleaning and disinfection changed the microbial communities present on field equipment, we found this did not completely eliminate the transfer of microbial taxa between gear and local soils. Field operations in the Dry Valleys are therefore likely contributing to the movement of locally adapted and valley-specific microbial communities. We haven’t yet determined the potential ecological impact of our findings. But these results clearly emphasise the importance of biosecurity monitoring and decontamination protocols across Antarctic field programmes. New Zealanders have accepted the need to disinfect boots to prevent the spread of pathogens such as kauri dieback disease. In Antarctica’s Dry Valleys, we need to strengthen contamination protocols to disinfect boots and field gear if more than one site is visited, while also upping biosecurity monitoring for microbes and other easily dispersed species. Angela (Ang) McGaughran receives funding from the Royal Society Te Apārangi and received proof-of-concept funding from Antarctica New Zealand for the microbial study.
