articles.content: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images If you’re like me, when you pick up a compass you can’t help but spin it this way and that, to see if you can trick it. It’s hard to resist experimenting with a spooky force we can’t see or feel ourselves. Yet it always turns the compass needle back towards north. Even in today’s high-tech world, compasses are useful navigation tools. A compass works without power, unlike GPS, and in any weather and lighting conditions, as opposed to navigation using the Sun, stars or landmarks. If you know which way north is, you can determine any direction. Like all cool phenomena, the explanation of how a compass works is not magic – it’s physics. And people have been making use of this particular aspect of physics for more than 2,000 years . A lodestone spoon The earliest versions of the compass were developed in ancient China. They were spoon-shaped and made of lodestones , pieces of the naturally magnetic mineral magnetite. When allowed to rotate freely, the spoon handle would align itself with a particular direction (north–south). This was used to organise and harmonise environments, as part of a practice you might know as feng shui . Model of a Han dynasty (206 BC–220 AD) south-indicating ladle. Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-NC-SA At the time, it was known that some materials were naturally magnetic – able to attract one another. However, it wasn’t clear exactly what was causing a compass to align itself north–south until 1600, when English physicist William Gilbert deduced that Earth itself acted as a giant magnet . An invisible field Like all magnets, Earth generates a magnetic field – an invisible region within which its magnetic forces act. Electricity and magnetism are closely connected. Together, they form one of the fundamental interactions in physics: electromagnetism . Magnetic fields can be created by electric currents, which are the movements of charged particles; a changing magnetic field can also induce an electrical current. Our planet spins around an axis once roughly every 24 hours, which is why we have a night and day cycle . The end points of this axis are the North Pole and the South Pole. Beneath Earth’s surface, in the outer core, electrically conducting liquid metals circulate in convective currents . This movement generates electrical currents. Paired with Earth’s rotation around its axis, these currents maintain a global-scale magnetic field . It extends out into space like a giant, invisible bubble, known as the magnetosphere. And it’s this global-scale magnetic field that allows a compass to work. Earth’s magnetic field is called the magnetosphere. NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio In modern compasses, a magnetised metal needle has replaced the lodestone spoon. That needle is mounted on a low-friction pivot so it has minimal resistance to the effects of external magnetic fields. As a result, unless there’s a magnet directly nearby, the needle will align itself with Earth’s magnetic north–south direction. If you’ve ever found that a compass needle didn’t perfectly align with north–south, it might be because it detected a localised magnetic field. Electrical devices such as your phone produce weak magnetic fields. These can affect a compass, causing it to deviate from Earth’s magnetic field. Watch what happens when a magnet is placed next to a compass. Which way does a compass really point? All magnets have two opposite points – a “north” pole and a “south” pole. If you have two magnets, opposite poles (north–south) will pull towards each other, while the same poles (south–south or north–north) will push away. The next bit will seem a little confusing, but it’s key to understand why compasses point towards the geographic north. Because opposites attract, the “north” arrow on a compass points towards the “south” pole of Earth’s global-scale magnetic field – the area where field lines point down into Earth’s surface. Despite it having a magnetic polarity of “south”, we call this spot the north magnetic pole because it’s located close to the geographic North Pole in the Arctic. Earth also has a magnetic south pole, and you guessed it – it’s located near the South Pole in Antarctica, while being the “north” counterpart of Earth’s magnetic field. Why compasses point towards the north. Useful in more ways than one The magnetic poles don’t align perfectly with the poles of Earth’s rotational axis. The reason for this is that Earth’s magnetic field is dynamic. The ever-changing motion of liquid metal in Earth’s outer core means the global magnetic field changes, too. In fact, the magnetic north and south poles slowly change their locations, and the entire magnetic field has even flipped its polarity in the past, making the two switch places. Earth’s magnetic field also acts as a protective barrier from space weather generated by our Sun: there’s a constant stream of charged particles coming our way, known as solar wind. The global magnetic field helps to shield Earth and our atmosphere. Mars, by contrast, no longer has a strong global-scale magnetic field to act as a protective shield. Interactions with solar wind have, over time, contributed to the loss of much of Mars’ atmosphere . So, the same invisible magnetic field that turns a compass needle also plays a much bigger role in helping to keep Earth our home . articles.content: Rob Hampson/Unsplash You search online for a new pair of running shoes. Later, while scrolling through Instagram, an ad appears for the very shoes you were considering. Perhaps you watched a video about travelling to Japan, and now your Facebook feed is full of flight deals and hotel offers. The timing can feel uncanny. Some people even wonder whether their phones are listening to private conversations . But advertising platforms don’t need to listen to know what might interest us. Our searches, clicks, purchases and other online activities can reveal far more than we realise. Australia’s digital duty of care bill , which is currently under Senate inquiry , would require online services to take steps to protect users from serious online harms. As part of this, the government introduced the My Feed, My Way initiative . It would give Australians the option to choose social media feeds that only show content from users they follow, as opposed to a feed full of algorithmically recommended content. However, these proposed controls don’t necessarily affect the advertisements appearing in the feeds. So even if we gain greater control over our social media feeds, what about the ads? You can control ads – to an extent Facebook and Instagram already allow users to influence the advertisements they see. Through Meta’s Accounts Centre , users can manage advertising preferences, select topics they want to see fewer advertisements about, and hide ads from particular advertisers. But this doesn’t guarantee the ads will completely disappear. On YouTube, Google’s My Ad Centre allows users to manage advertising topics, limit certain sensitive categories (such as gambling or alcohol) and turn off personalised advertising. TikTok also provides advertising controls , including options to manage advertising topics, mute advertisers and review activity shared by advertising partners. These settings provide useful choices, but there is an important limitation. Changing the ads you see doesn’t necessarily change what information a platform collects about you. For example, selecting fewer fitness advertisements on Instagram doesn’t prevent Meta from receiving information about your visits to fitness websites. To understand why, we need to look at where advertising information comes from. How do platforms know what interests us? Online platforms that serve ads collect information about our online activities, both within their apps and from other websites. Businesses may use tracking technologies, such as the Meta Pixel , to share information about your visit with Meta. It’s essentially a trail of data you create while browsing the internet. That information can help advertisers reach people who’ve previously shown interest in their products, and deliver targeted ads to them. Platforms also use our in-app activities to predict our interests and personalise ads. This can make advertisements appear remarkably accurate – to the point where you might think they’re actually listening to you. In June , Meta announced it was expanding how it uses information shared by other businesses. Previously used to personalise ads, this data will now also help to personalise feeds and AI responses: We already use this data – like games you play or purchases you make on other websites – to make the ads you see more relevant. In the future, we’ll use this information to personalise other parts of your experience. Meta also announced users will be able to control whether its platforms can use this data to personalise the content they’re served. But there’s a distinction between restricting how information is used and preventing businesses from collecting and passing it on in the first place. What does Australian law say? Australia already has privacy laws that apply to targeted advertising. Under the current privacy act , organisations covered by the Australian Privacy Principles must comply with requirements governing the use and disclosure of personal information for direct marketing. These include circumstances in which individuals can request that their personal information no longer be used or disclosed for direct marketing. However, these protections are not equivalent to a universal ban on online tracking or personalised advertising. The proposed digital duty of care legislation primarily addresses online safety and user empowerment. Its provisions for controlling our feeds don’t explicitly establish a right to disable targeted advertising. However, the government is also currently revising our privacy laws. The draft bill proposes a “fair and reasonable” test for collecting, using and disclosing personal information. Essentially, it asks: even if the person consented, did the organisation handle the data fairly? Organisations will also have to provide ways for people to “easily” opt out of direct marketing, the definition of which has been broadened to include targeted ads online. However, this privacy law reform is yet to be introduced to parliament. What can we do to protect our information? Start by reviewing advertising preferences on any big tech platforms you use, such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok or Google. Look beyond hitting the “hide” button on individual ads and instead examine the settings that control how your data is used. Check your phone’s app-tracking permissions and your browser’s privacy settings. Where available, restrict third-party tracking and reject unnecessary advertising cookies. Review the activity histories associated with your online accounts and delete information you no longer want stored, where the service allows it. Australia’s proposed reforms could give us greater choice over our social media experience. Yet choosing what appears in our feeds is only one part of the problem. Real control over advertising means having a say not just in which ads appear, but in what information is collected and shared to put them there. articles.author: Nils Pratley
articles.content: The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes. This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words. Continue reading...

articles.content: Insurance premiums have increased by nearly 50% in five years, turning basic coverage into an unaffordable luxury for some Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The cost of home insurance has surged at twice the pace of inflation over the past five years, leaving homeowners like Matthew with an impossible choice: pay up to $8,000 a year for a policy or go uninsured. For Matthew, who lives in regional Victoria and asked to be identified by his first name only, skyrocketing premiums have turned basic coverage into an unaffordable luxury, especially after his insurer denied a previous claim and cancelled his policy. Continue reading...

articles.content: Every year I receive a letter from the daughter of a patient I treated. It’s an act of unbelievable grace in a job that often feels thankless Many years ago, in early November, I received a note. It read: “Dear Doctor, Dad would have been 78 years old today. Of course, no amount of time would have been enough. We think of him and miss him every day.” Continue reading...

articles.author: Rosamund Brennan
articles.content: Eighty years after hundreds of Aboriginal workers walked off Pilbara stations, a trove of photos found beneath a wardrobe documents what happened next Warning: This article contains images of and references to Indigenous Australians who have died Troy Eaton lives in Pippingarra, near Port Hedland, where the Pilbara’s multibillion-dollar mining industry looms large. “It’s a mecca of mining,” says the Nyamal man. But his family’s mining history stretches back long before the arrival of today’s resources giants. In September, Eaton took the long drive from Pippingarra to Perth to see some of those early pioneers: his ancestors, who established their own mining ventures in the Pilbara some 80 years ago. Continue reading...

articles.author: Samuel Gibbs Consumer technology editor
articles.content: Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out. It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros. Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz) Processor: Apple M6 RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB Storage: 1, 2 or 4TB SSD Operating system: macOS 26.4 Tahoe Camera: 12MP Centre Stage Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones Dimensions: 221.2 x 312.6 x 15.5mm Weight: 1.55kg Continue reading...
